questions.text: What are vitamins?
questions.answer: Organic compounds, essential for life, cannot be synthesized by the body, do not enter the structure of tissues or get oxidized by them, and are needed in very small amounts.
questions.explanation: Vitamins are micronutrients that function primarily as coenzymes or precursors to coenzymes. Despite being required in trace amounts, their absence leads to characteristic deficiency diseases. They are classified as fat-soluble (A, D, E, K) or water-soluble (B complex and C).

questions.text: What are vitamers?
questions.answer: Different chemical forms of the same vitamin. Example: Vitamin D has two vitamers — D₂ (ergocalciferol) and D₃ (cholecalciferol).
questions.explanation: Vitamers are structurally related compounds that exhibit the same vitamin activity. They may differ in potency or bioavailability. The body can often interconvert vitamers or utilize multiple forms for the same biological function.

questions.text: What are pro-vitamins?
questions.answer: Precursors of vitamins that are converted into active vitamins inside the body. Example: 7-dehydrocholesterol is the pro-vitamin of D₃.
questions.explanation: Pro-vitamins are inactive precursor compounds that require metabolic activation to become functional vitamins. Another classic example is β-carotene (pro-vitamin A), which is cleaved in the intestinal mucosa to yield retinal (vitamin A aldehyde).

questions.text: What are fat-soluble vitamins?
questions.answer: Vitamins A, D, E, and K.
questions.explanation: Fat-soluble vitamins are absorbed alongside dietary fats via the lymphatic system and are stored in the liver and adipose tissue. Because they accumulate in the body, excess intake (especially of vitamins A and D) can lead to toxicity (hypervitaminosis). They require bile salts for proper intestinal absorption.

questions.text: What are the sources of Vitamin A?
questions.answer: Carrots, green leafy vegetables, and fish liver oil.
questions.explanation: Vitamin A (retinol) is obtained from two dietary sources: (1) preformed vitamin A (retinol/retinyl esters) from animal sources such as liver, fish liver oil, egg yolk, and dairy; and (2) provitamin A carotenoids (primarily β-carotene) from plant sources such as carrots, sweet potatoes, and dark leafy greens.

questions.text: What is the pro-vitamin A?
questions.answer: β-carotene, present in plants.
questions.explanation: β-carotene is the most potent provitamin A carotenoid. It is a symmetrical molecule that is cleaved centrally by β-carotene 15,15'-dioxygenase in the intestinal mucosal cells to yield two molecules of all-trans retinal, which is then reduced to retinol (vitamin A alcohol).

questions.text: What is the major function of Vitamin A?
questions.answer: Night vision.
questions.explanation: Vitamin A (in the form of 11-cis retinal) is an essential component of rhodopsin, the photosensitive pigment in rod cells of the retina. Rhodopsin enables vision in dim light. Vitamin A deficiency impairs rhodopsin regeneration, leading to night blindness (nyctalopia) as the earliest clinical manifestation.

questions.text: What are the other biological roles of Vitamin A?
questions.answer: Normal maintenance of epithelium and skin, glycoprotein synthesis, reproduction, cell differentiation, and antioxidant role.
questions.explanation: Beyond vision, vitamin A (as retinoic acid) acts as a transcription factor ligand through nuclear retinoic acid receptors (RARs), regulating gene expression involved in: epithelial cell differentiation and integrity, mucus secretion, spermatogenesis and embryonic development, immune function, and antioxidant defense (β-carotene quenches singlet oxygen).

questions.text: What is the visual cycle?
questions.answer: Rhodopsin (opsin + 11-cis retinal) absorbs light → 11-cis retinal isomerizes to all-trans retinal → membrane permeability of rod cells changes → calcium ions exit the cell → nerve impulse is generated in the optic nerve → brain perceives light.
questions.explanation: The visual cycle (phototransduction): Rhodopsin in rod cells consists of the protein opsin covalently bound to 11-cis retinal. Photon absorption triggers isomerization to all-trans retinal, causing conformational change in opsin (forming metarhodopsin II), which activates transducin (a G-protein), leading to cGMP hydrolysis, closure of Na⁺ channels, hyperpolarization of the rod cell, and generation of an optic nerve impulse interpreted as light by the brain.

questions.text: What causes the nerve impulse in the retina?
questions.answer: Isomerization (conversion) of 11-cis retinal to all-trans retinal upon light exposure.
questions.explanation: This photoisomerization is the primary photochemical event in vision. The change in retinal geometry triggers a cascade of conformational changes in rhodopsin, activating the visual transduction pathway that ultimately generates an action potential in the optic nerve.

questions.text: How is 11-cis retinal regenerated?
questions.answer: All-trans retinal is transported to the liver → converted to all-trans retinol → isomerized to 11-cis retinol → oxidized back to 11-cis retinal.
questions.explanation: Regeneration of 11-cis retinal (the visual cycle dark reactions): All-trans retinal released from bleached rhodopsin is reduced to all-trans retinol by alcohol dehydrogenase, transported to the RPE (retinal pigment epithelium) cells, isomerized to 11-cis retinol by retinol isomerase, and then oxidized to 11-cis retinal, which recombines with opsin to regenerate rhodopsin.

questions.text: What are the enzymes required for the regeneration of 11-cis retinal?
questions.answer: Alcohol dehydrogenase and retinol isomerase.
questions.explanation: Alcohol dehydrogenase (NAD⁺-dependent) catalyzes the interconversion between retinal (aldehyde) and retinol (alcohol). Retinol isomerase (also called RPE65 in the retinal pigment epithelium) catalyzes the all-trans to 11-cis isomerization, which is the critical step in rhodopsin regeneration and sustained dark adaptation.

questions.text: How is Vitamin A absorbed?
questions.answer: In intestinal mucosal cells, β-carotene is cleaved to retinal → re-esterified with palmitic acid → transported via lymphatics to the liver, where 90% of body vitamin A is stored.
questions.explanation: Dietary retinyl esters are hydrolyzed in the intestinal lumen by pancreatic retinyl ester hydrolase. Free retinol enters mucosal cells, is re-esterified (mainly with palmitate), packaged into chylomicrons, and transported via lymph to the liver. The liver stores vitamin A as retinyl esters in stellate (Ito) cells and releases retinol bound to retinol-binding protein (RBP) into the bloodstream.

questions.text: How does Vitamin A circulate in blood?
questions.answer: In association with retinol-binding protein (RBP), which is formed by the liver.
questions.explanation: Retinol is released from the liver bound to RBP (retinol-binding protein), a 21 kDa transport protein synthesized by hepatocytes. The RBP–retinol complex circulates in plasma associated with transthyretin (prealbumin), which prevents renal filtration of the small RBP molecule. RBP synthesis is zinc-dependent and reduced in protein malnutrition.

questions.text: What are the deficiency manifestations of Vitamin A?
questions.answer: Night blindness, xerophthalmia, keratomalacia, and keratinization of epithelium leading to roughness of skin (goose skin) and mucous membranes.
questions.explanation: Vitamin A deficiency manifestations progress in severity: (1) Night blindness (earliest sign) — impaired rhodopsin regeneration; (2) Xerophthalmia — conjunctival and corneal dryness with Bitot's spots; (3) Keratomalacia — corneal softening and ulceration, may lead to blindness; (4) Keratinization — replacement of mucus-secreting columnar epithelium with stratified squamous keratinized epithelium, increasing susceptibility to infections throughout the respiratory, GI, and urinary tracts.

questions.text: Why is overdosage of vitamins A and D toxic?
questions.answer: Because these vitamins are transported bound to albumin. When their concentration exceeds albumin's binding capacity, free vitamins are released into blood and exert toxic effects on tissues.
questions.explanation: Fat-soluble vitamins A and D are stored in the liver and adipose tissue and are not readily excreted in urine. Chronic excessive intake leads to accumulation. Hypervitaminosis A causes headache, hepatotoxicity, teratogenicity, and bone pain. Hypervitaminosis D causes hypercalcemia, leading to calcification of soft tissues, nephrocalcinosis, and cardiac arrhythmias.

questions.text: What is the daily requirement of Vitamin A?
questions.answer: 5000 IU/day.
questions.explanation: The recommended daily allowance (RDA) for vitamin A in adults is approximately 700–900 μg RAE (retinol activity equivalents) per day, which corresponds to approximately 2300–3000 IU. The older figure of 5000 IU/day is a commonly cited traditional unit. Pregnant and lactating women have higher requirements.

questions.text: How is cholecalciferol (D₃) synthesized?
questions.answer: From the provitamin 7-dehydrocholesterol present in subcutaneous fat, by the action of ultraviolet (UV) rays from sunlight.
questions.explanation: UV-B radiation (wavelength 290–315 nm) photolytically cleaves the B ring of 7-dehydrocholesterol in the skin to form pre-vitamin D₃, which undergoes thermal isomerization to cholecalciferol (vitamin D₃). The process is self-limiting — prolonged UV exposure causes photodegradation of pre-vitamin D₃ and vitamin D₃ to inactive products, preventing toxicity from sun exposure alone.

questions.text: How is Vitamin D activated?
questions.answer: Cholecalciferol (D₃) → liver (25-hydroxylation) → 25-hydroxycholecalciferol (25-HCC) → kidney (1-hydroxylation) → 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (DHCC) — the active form.
questions.explanation: Vitamin D activation requires two sequential hydroxylation steps: (1) In the liver: vitamin D 25-hydroxylase (CYP2R1) converts D₃ to 25-OH-D₃ (calcidiol) — the major circulating form used for assessing vitamin D status. (2) In the kidney: 1α-hydroxylase (CYP27B1) converts 25-OH-D₃ to 1,25-(OH)₂D₃ (calcitriol) — the biologically active hormone. Renal 1α-hydroxylase is stimulated by PTH, hypocalcemia, and hypophosphatemia.

questions.text: What is calcitriol?
questions.answer: The active form of Vitamin D — 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol. It contains three hydroxyl groups at positions 1, 3, and 25, hence the name calcitriol.
questions.explanation: Calcitriol [1,25-(OH)₂D₃] is the most potent biologically active metabolite of vitamin D. It acts as a steroid hormone, binding to the nuclear vitamin D receptor (VDR) and regulating transcription of target genes in the intestine, kidney, bone, and parathyroid gland. Its primary action is to increase serum calcium by enhancing intestinal calcium absorption, stimulating renal calcium reabsorption, and (at high doses) promoting bone resorption.

questions.text: Which vitamins act as pro-hormones?
questions.answer: Vitamins A and D.
questions.explanation: Vitamin D is converted to calcitriol, which acts as a steroid hormone by binding to nuclear VDRs and regulating gene transcription. Vitamin A (as retinoic acid) similarly binds to nuclear receptors (RAR and RXR) to modulate gene expression. Both vitamins regulate growth, differentiation, and metabolism at the genomic level, analogous to classical steroid and thyroid hormones.

questions.text: What is the function of Vitamin D?
questions.answer: Increases intestinal absorption of calcium → normalizes serum calcium levels. Also increases mineralization of bone.
questions.explanation: Calcitriol's primary function is calcium homeostasis: (1) Intestine: upregulates calbindin synthesis, increasing Ca²⁺ absorption; (2) Kidney: promotes Ca²⁺ and phosphate reabsorption; (3) Bone: at physiological levels, promotes mineralization by maintaining adequate Ca²⁺ × PO₄³⁻ ion product; at pharmacological levels, stimulates osteoclast-mediated bone resorption. Overall goal: maintain serum Ca²⁺ within the normal range (2.1–2.6 mmol/L).

questions.text: How does calcitriol increase absorption of calcium?
questions.answer: By stimulating the synthesis of calbindin (calcium-binding protein) in the intestinal mucosal cells.
questions.explanation: Calcitriol binds to the VDR in intestinal epithelial cells, forming a VDR–RXR heterodimer that acts as a transcription factor. This complex binds to vitamin D response elements (VDREs) in the promoter of the calbindin gene, stimulating its transcription. Calbindin facilitates transcellular calcium transport from the intestinal lumen to the bloodstream by binding Ca²⁺ and ferrying it across the cell.

questions.text: What is the mechanism of calcium absorption?
questions.answer: Calcitriol binds to VDR in intestinal mucosal cells → stimulates DNA transcription of specific genes → synthesis of calbindin (calcium-binding protein) → increased calcium absorption.
questions.explanation: The mechanism involves: (1) Luminal uptake of Ca²⁺ via TRPV6 (transient receptor potential cation channel) at the apical membrane; (2) Intracellular transport bound to calbindin-D9k; (3) Basolateral extrusion via PMCA1b (plasma membrane Ca²⁺-ATPase) and NCX1 (Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger). All three components are upregulated by calcitriol at the transcriptional level.

questions.text: Explain why active Vitamin D is considered a hormone.
questions.answer: Because its mechanism of action — stimulation of DNA transcription — is similar to that of steroid hormones.
questions.explanation: Calcitriol fulfills the classic criteria of a hormone: (1) it is synthesized in one organ (kidney); (2) released into blood; (3) acts on distant target organs (intestine, bone, kidney); (4) exerts its effect by binding to an intracellular nuclear receptor (VDR) that regulates gene transcription — identical to the mechanism of steroid, thyroid, and retinoic acid hormones. Its serum levels are tightly regulated by a feedback system involving PTH and serum calcium.

questions.text: Which vitamin is steroid in nature?
questions.answer: Vitamin D — it is the only vitamin with a steroidal structure.
questions.explanation: Vitamin D is derived from 7-dehydrocholesterol, a sterol precursor. Its structure retains the steroid nucleus (cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene ring system) with an opened B ring following UV irradiation. This structural relationship to steroids explains its hormone-like mechanism of action through nuclear receptors.

questions.text: What is the relationship between parathyroid hormone (PTH) and calcium metabolism?
questions.answer: Hypocalcemia → PTH release → activation of renal 1α-hydroxylase → conversion of 25-OH-D₃ to 1,25-(OH)₂D₃ (calcitriol) → increased intestinal calcium absorption.
questions.explanation: PTH is the primary regulator of calcitriol synthesis. The feedback loop: low serum Ca²⁺ → chief cells of parathyroid gland secrete PTH → PTH acts on renal proximal tubule cells to upregulate CYP27B1 (1α-hydroxylase) → increased calcitriol production → enhanced intestinal Ca²⁺ absorption and renal Ca²⁺ reabsorption → serum Ca²⁺ rises → PTH secretion suppressed (negative feedback).

questions.text: How is Vitamin D deficiency manifested?
questions.answer: Rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults — both characterized by demineralization of bones.
questions.explanation: Rickets (children): defective mineralization of growing bone and cartilage → soft, deformable bones → bowing of legs, widening of epiphyses (rachitic rosary), craniotabes, delayed fontanelle closure, and Harrison's sulcus. Osteomalacia (adults): inadequate mineralization of osteoid matrix → bone pain, tenderness, proximal muscle weakness, and pathological fractures (pseudofractures/Looser zones on X-ray).

questions.text: In renal disease, oral doses of Vitamin D may not be effective. Why?
questions.answer: Because the final activation step (1α-hydroxylation at position 1) of vitamin D occurs in the kidney. In renal disease, this conversion is impaired.
questions.explanation: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) leads to reduced 1α-hydroxylase activity in the proximal tubule, resulting in deficient calcitriol production despite adequate 25-OH-D₃ levels. This causes renal osteodystrophy. Treatment therefore requires administration of active calcitriol (1,25-(OH)₂D₃) or its analogue alfacalcidol (1α-OH-D₃) directly, bypassing the need for renal activation.

questions.text: What are the causes of rickets?
questions.answer: Underexposure to sunlight, chronic renal failure, and liver diseases.
questions.explanation: Causes of rickets include: (1) Inadequate sunlight exposure (dietary deficiency alone is rarely sufficient); (2) Chronic renal failure — impaired 1α-hydroxylation; (3) Liver disease — impaired 25-hydroxylation; (4) Malabsorption syndromes; (5) Hereditary vitamin D-resistant rickets (VDR mutations); (6) X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets (PHEX gene mutation causing FGF23 excess and phosphate wasting).

questions.text: What vitamins are important for bones?
questions.answer: Vitamin D, Vitamin A, and Vitamin C.
questions.explanation: Bone health requires: Vitamin D — for calcium absorption and bone mineralization; Vitamin A — for osteoblast and osteoclast differentiation and bone remodeling; Vitamin C — for collagen synthesis (the organic matrix of bone is primarily type I collagen; deficiency causes scurvy with bone fragility and subperiosteal hemorrhage). Additionally, Vitamin K is critical for γ-carboxylation of osteocalcin, a bone matrix protein essential for mineralization.

questions.text: What is the daily requirement of Vitamin D?
questions.answer: 400 IU/day.
questions.explanation: The traditional recommended daily intake of vitamin D is 400 IU (10 μg)/day. Current guidelines (particularly for adults, older individuals, and those with limited sun exposure) recommend higher intakes of 600–2000 IU/day. The tolerable upper intake level is 4000 IU/day for adults, above which hypercalcemia and toxicity may occur.

questions.text: What is the chemical nature of Vitamin E?
questions.answer: α-Tocopherol.
questions.explanation: Vitamin E is a collective term for a group of fat-soluble compounds including tocopherols (α, β, γ, δ) and tocotrienols. α-Tocopherol is the most biologically active form and the predominant form in human tissues. It has a chroman head group (hydroxyl group on a benzene ring) and a phytyl tail that anchors it in cell membranes, where it exerts its antioxidant activity.

questions.text: What is the function of Vitamin E?
questions.answer: Antioxidant.
questions.explanation: α-Tocopherol is the body's primary lipid-soluble antioxidant. It protects polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) in cell membranes and plasma lipoproteins from peroxidation by scavenging lipid peroxyl radicals (LOO•), donating a hydrogen atom to form a tocopheroxyl radical. The tocopheroxyl radical is then reduced back to tocopherol by vitamin C (ascorbate) in the aqueous phase — a synergistic antioxidant interaction.

questions.text: What is the relationship between Vitamin E and heart disease?
questions.answer: Vitamin E acts as an antioxidant. It prevents oxidation of LDL. Oxidized LDL promotes atherosclerosis.
questions.explanation: Oxidative modification of LDL is a key initiating event in atherogenesis. Oxidized LDL is taken up by macrophage scavenger receptors (bypassing normal LDL receptor feedback), forming foam cells that accumulate in arterial walls, initiating atherosclerotic plaques. α-Tocopherol within LDL particles inhibits lipid peroxidation, potentially reducing LDL oxidation and cardiovascular risk. However, large clinical trials have yielded mixed results regarding vitamin E supplementation and CVD outcomes.

questions.text: What is the relationship between selenium and Vitamin E?
questions.answer: They act synergistically as antioxidants.
questions.explanation: Selenium is a component of glutathione peroxidase (GPx), an enzyme that detoxifies hydrogen peroxide and lipid hydroperoxides using glutathione (GSH). Vitamin E prevents lipid peroxidation at the membrane level, while selenium-dependent GPx destroys the resulting hydroperoxides in the aqueous phase. Both deficiencies can lead to similar pathologies (e.g., cardiomyopathy, skeletal muscle damage), and each can partially compensate for the deficiency of the other.

questions.text: What are the sources of Vitamin E?
questions.answer: Vegetables and seed oils: sunflower oil, safflower oil, cottonseed oil, and palm oil.
questions.explanation: Vitamin E is found predominantly in plant-derived foods rich in unsaturated fats. The richest sources include wheat germ oil, sunflower oil, safflower oil, and almonds. Green leafy vegetables, nuts, and seeds also provide significant amounts. Animal products generally contain lower amounts. Notably, foods rich in PUFAs tend to contain proportionally higher vitamin E, as PUFAs are the main substrate that vitamin E protects from oxidation.

questions.text: What is the normal daily requirement of Vitamin E?
questions.answer: 15 IU/day.
questions.explanation: The current RDA for vitamin E in adults is 15 mg/day of α-tocopherol (approximately 22.4 IU for natural d-α-tocopherol or 33.3 IU for synthetic dl-α-tocopherol). Requirements increase with higher PUFA intake. The tolerable upper limit is 1000 mg/day; excess vitamin E can act as a pro-oxidant and may interfere with vitamin K-dependent clotting factors, increasing bleeding risk.

questions.text: What is the chemical nature of Vitamin K?
questions.answer: Naphthoquinone derivative.
questions.explanation: Vitamin K exists in two natural forms: K₁ (phylloquinone) from plants and K₂ (menaquinone) from bacteria. Both share a 2-methyl-1,4-naphthoquinone (menadione) core structure, differing only in their side chains at position 3. The naphthoquinone ring undergoes reversible reduction/oxidation that is essential for its enzymatic role in the γ-carboxylation cycle.

questions.text: What is menadione?
questions.answer: A synthetic, water-soluble form of Vitamin K widely used in clinical practice.
questions.explanation: Menadione (vitamin K₃) is 2-methyl-1,4-naphthoquinone — the unsubstituted parent compound of the vitamin K family. Unlike the natural fat-soluble K₁ and K₂, menadione is water-soluble and does not require bile salts for absorption, making it useful in conditions of fat malabsorption (e.g., obstructive jaundice). It is alkylated in vivo to form MK-4 (menaquinone-4), the active form.

questions.text: What is the function of Vitamin K?
questions.answer: (1) Synthesis of blood clotting factors II (prothrombin), VII, IX, and X in the liver via γ-carboxylation. (2) Maintenance of osteocalcin (calcium-binding protein) synthesis in bone.
questions.explanation: Vitamin K is an essential cofactor for the enzyme γ-glutamyl carboxylase, which converts specific glutamate (Glu) residues to γ-carboxyglutamate (Gla) residues in vitamin K-dependent proteins. Gla residues chelate Ca²⁺ ions, enabling coagulation factors to bind phospholipid surfaces on activated platelets — a prerequisite for clot formation. Proteins C, S, and Z are also vitamin K-dependent anticoagulants. Osteocalcin's Gla residues bind hydroxyapatite, facilitating bone mineralization.

questions.text: In which conditions can Vitamin K deficiency occur?
questions.answer: Obstructive jaundice, antibiotic therapy, neonatal period, and prolonged use of dicumarol.
questions.explanation: Causes of vitamin K deficiency: (1) Obstructive jaundice — bile salts absent, impaired fat-soluble vitamin absorption; (2) Broad-spectrum antibiotics — eliminate gut bacteria (the source of K₂/menaquinone); (3) Neonates — sterile gut at birth, no bacterial K₂, low placental transfer, low breast milk content → hemorrhagic disease of the newborn (prevented by routine vitamin K₁ injection at birth); (4) Dicumarol/warfarin — blocks vitamin K epoxide reductase, depleting active vitamin K.

questions.text: Why is bleeding tendency common in obstructive jaundice?
questions.answer: Bile salts (essential for absorption of fat-soluble vitamin K) are reduced in obstructive jaundice. This impairs vitamin K absorption, leading to defective synthesis of coagulation factors.
questions.explanation: In obstructive jaundice, bile flow into the duodenum is blocked, leading to steatorrhea and malabsorption of all fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K). Vitamin K deficiency results in failure to γ-carboxylate prothrombin (factor II) and factors VII, IX, and X in the liver, impairing the coagulation cascade and producing a bleeding diathesis. Prothrombin time (PT) is prolonged. Parenteral vitamin K administration corrects the coagulopathy.

questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of dicumarol?
questions.answer: It competitively inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase.
questions.explanation: During γ-carboxylation, vitamin K hydroquinone (KH₂) is oxidized to vitamin K epoxide (KO). Vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKOR, encoded by VKORC1) normally recycles KO back to KH₂, regenerating active vitamin K. Dicumarol (and its derivative warfarin) are structural analogues of vitamin K that competitively inhibit VKOR, depleting the active KH₂ pool and impairing γ-carboxylation of clotting factors.

questions.text: Dicumarol is used for what purpose?
questions.answer: To prevent intravascular thrombosis.
questions.explanation: Dicumarol (bishydroxycoumarin) and its derivative warfarin are oral anticoagulants used clinically to prevent thromboembolic disorders including deep vein thrombosis (DVT), pulmonary embolism, atrial fibrillation-associated stroke, and mechanical heart valve thrombosis. They reduce synthesis of functional vitamin K-dependent clotting factors, thereby increasing clotting time (INR/PT) and reducing thrombotic risk.

questions.text: Excess dicumarol will produce what?
questions.answer: Bleeding tendency (hemorrhage).
questions.explanation: Overdose of dicumarol/warfarin causes excessive anticoagulation (supratherapeutic INR), manifesting as spontaneous bleeding — ecchymoses, hematuria, GI hemorrhage, intracranial bleeding, and retroperitoneal hematoma. Treatment: vitamin K₁ (phytonadione) administration reverses warfarin effect within 12–24 hours. In severe hemorrhage, fresh frozen plasma (FFP) or prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) provides immediate factor replacement.

questions.text: Which substance inhibits Vitamin K?
questions.answer: Dicumarol.
questions.explanation: Dicumarol and warfarin are the prototype vitamin K antagonists. They do not directly inhibit vitamin K itself but block its regeneration by inhibiting VKOR, creating functional vitamin K deficiency. Other vitamin K antagonists include phenindione and acenocoumarol. All act as anticoagulants by depleting active vitamin K, preventing γ-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X.

questions.text: Why is Vitamin K deficient in neonates?
questions.answer: The neonatal intestine in the first week of life is sterile — it contains no bacteria that synthesize vitamin K.
questions.explanation: Neonates are at risk for vitamin K deficiency hemorrhage (VKDH) due to: (1) Sterile gut — no intestinal bacteria to synthesize menaquinone (K₂); (2) Low placental transfer of vitamin K; (3) Low vitamin K content in breast milk; (4) Immature liver with reduced synthesis capacity. This is prevented by prophylactic intramuscular vitamin K₁ (1 mg) given at birth — a universal neonatal practice.

questions.text: Bleeding tendency is common in the deficiency of which substances?
questions.answer: Vitamin K, Vitamin C, and platelets.
questions.explanation: Hemorrhagic diathesis results from: (1) Vitamin K deficiency — impaired γ-carboxylation of coagulation factors II, VII, IX, X → defective secondary hemostasis (coagulation); (2) Vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) — impaired collagen synthesis → vascular fragility, perifollicular hemorrhage, bleeding gums; (3) Thrombocytopenia (low platelet count) — impaired primary hemostasis (platelet plug formation). Each mechanism affects a different component of the hemostatic system.

questions.text: What are water-soluble vitamins?
questions.answer: Vitamin C and the B complex group (11 vitamins).
questions.explanation: Water-soluble vitamins include: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) and the B complex vitamins: B₁ (thiamine), B₂ (riboflavin), B₃ (niacin), B₅ (pantothenic acid), B₆ (pyridoxine), B₇ (biotin), B₉ (folic acid), B₁₂ (cobalamin), plus choline, inositol, and lipoic acid (sometimes included). Unlike fat-soluble vitamins, water-soluble vitamins are not stored in large amounts (exception: B₁₂) and excess is excreted in urine, making daily dietary intake essential.

questions.text: Explain why all vitamins of the B complex are grouped together.
questions.answer: Because they all share the same food sources: yeast, liver, egg yolk, milk, and whole grain cereals.
questions.explanation: The B complex vitamins are grouped together not because of structural or functional similarity, but because of their common dietary sources and their shared role as coenzymes in cellular metabolism. They are all water-soluble, heat-sensitive, and participate in enzymatic reactions involving energy metabolism, nucleic acid synthesis, and amino acid metabolism. Deficiency of one B vitamin often coexists with deficiency of others due to shared food sources.

questions.text: What are good sources of thiamine (Vitamin B₁)?
questions.answer: Whole grain cereals, whole-wheat flour, unpolished rice, and yeast.
questions.explanation: Thiamine is concentrated in the outer bran and germ layers of cereal grains. Milling and polishing of rice removes these layers, drastically reducing thiamine content — a major cause of beriberi in populations relying on polished white rice. Other sources include legumes, pork, and organ meats. Thiamine is heat-labile and destroyed by prolonged cooking, alkaline conditions, and thiaminases present in raw fish.

questions.text: Which vitamin is required for oxidative decarboxylation reactions?
questions.answer: Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) — the active coenzyme form of Vitamin B₁.
questions.explanation: Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) is the coenzyme form of thiamine, formed by the addition of two phosphate groups to thiamine by thiamine pyrophosphokinase. TPP functions as a coenzyme for α-keto acid dehydrogenase complexes, where it acts as an 'active aldehyde' carrier, stabilizing carbanion intermediates formed after decarboxylation. The key reactive group is the C2 carbon of the thiazolium ring, which forms a covalent adduct with the α-keto acid substrate.

questions.text: Which enzymes require thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP)?
questions.answer: Pyruvate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and transketolase.
questions.explanation: TPP-dependent enzymes: (1) Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) — converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA (link between glycolysis and TCA cycle); (2) α-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex — converts α-ketoglutarate to succinyl-CoA (TCA cycle step 4); (3) Transketolase — transfers two-carbon units in the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP). In thiamine deficiency, erythrocyte transketolase activity is used as a diagnostic biomarker.

questions.text: What are the functions of Vitamin B₁ (thiamine)?
questions.answer: (1) Oxidative decarboxylation of α-keto acids (e.g., pyruvate → acetyl-CoA). (2) Transketolation in the pentose phosphate pathway. (3) Essential for nerve conduction and structure of nerve membranes.
questions.explanation: TPP's metabolic roles encompass: (1) Energy metabolism — PDC and α-KGDH link glycolysis and amino acid catabolism to the TCA cycle; (2) Pentose phosphate pathway — transketolase generates ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotide synthesis and NADPH for reductive biosynthesis; (3) Neurological function — thiamine triphosphate (TTP) regulates chloride channel activity in nerve membranes. In deficiency, accumulation of pyruvate and lactate impairs brain energy metabolism, causing neurological symptoms.

questions.text: In thiamine deficiency, what alterations are seen in blood?
questions.answer: Increased pyruvic acid level and increased transketolase activity (with TPP stimulation).
questions.explanation: In thiamine deficiency: (1) Pyruvate accumulates because pyruvate dehydrogenase (TPP-dependent) cannot convert it to acetyl-CoA → elevated blood pyruvate and lactate → lactic acidosis; (2) Erythrocyte transketolase activity is low in vivo but shows a large percentage increase (>25% 'TPP effect') when TPP is added in vitro — this is the most sensitive and specific laboratory test for thiamine deficiency.

questions.text: Beriberi is due to the deficiency of which vitamin?
questions.answer: Vitamin B₁ (thiamine).
questions.explanation: Beriberi presents in two main forms: (1) Dry beriberi — peripheral neuropathy with symmetrical sensory and motor deficits, muscle wasting, and foot/wrist drop; (2) Wet beriberi — high-output cardiac failure with cardiomegaly, tachycardia, and peripheral edema due to vasodilation from pyruvate accumulation. Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (in alcoholics) is a neurological emergency involving ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and confabulation, treated urgently with IV thiamine.

questions.text: Chronic alcoholism may lead to the deficiency of which vitamin?
questions.answer: Vitamin B₁ (thiamine).
questions.explanation: Alcoholics are at high risk for thiamine deficiency due to: (1) Inadequate dietary intake (calories from alcohol replace nutritious food); (2) Impaired intestinal absorption of thiamine (ethanol inhibits thiamine transporters THTR1 and THTR2); (3) Reduced hepatic storage and phosphorylation to TPP; (4) Increased metabolic demand. This leads to Wernicke's encephalopathy (acute: ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, confusion) and Korsakoff's psychosis (chronic: anterograde amnesia, confabulation).

questions.text: What is the daily requirement of Vitamin B₁ (thiamine)?
questions.answer: 1.5 mg/day.
questions.explanation: Thiamine requirements are proportional to carbohydrate intake and energy expenditure (approximately 0.5 mg per 1000 kcal). The RDA for adults is 1.1–1.2 mg/day. Higher intakes are needed during pregnancy, lactation, fever, hyperthyroidism, and high-carbohydrate diets. Thiamine has no known toxicity even at high doses, as excess is readily excreted in urine.

questions.text: What is the coenzyme function of riboflavin (B₂)?
questions.answer: Riboflavin serves as the precursor for FMN and FAD — coenzymes for flavoprotein enzymes involved in oxidation-reduction reactions.
questions.explanation: Riboflavin is phosphorylated to FMN (flavin mononucleotide) by flavokinase, and FMN is combined with AMP by FAD synthetase to form FAD. Both FMN and FAD function as prosthetic groups of flavoproteins, accepting two electrons and two protons (as FMNH₂ and FADH₂) from substrate oxidation and transferring them to the electron transport chain (ETC) or other acceptors. Unlike NAD⁺, flavin coenzymes are tightly (often covalently) bound to their apoenzymes.

questions.text: What is the importance of Vitamin B₂ (riboflavin)?
questions.answer: Riboflavin enters the structure of FMN and FAD, which are coenzymes that act as hydrogen (electron) carriers in oxidation-reduction reactions.
questions.explanation: FAD and FMN are essential electron carriers in cellular respiration. FADH₂, generated in the TCA cycle (succinate dehydrogenase) and β-oxidation (acyl-CoA dehydrogenase), donates its electrons directly to CoQ (ubiquinone) in the ETC, yielding approximately 1.5 ATP per FADH₂. Riboflavin deficiency impairs energy metabolism and causes accumulation of reduced metabolites.

questions.text: What are the FAD-dependent enzymes?
questions.answer: Succinate dehydrogenase, acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, xanthine oxidase, glutathione reductase, glycine cleavage system, pyruvate dehydrogenase, and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.
questions.explanation: FAD-dependent enzymes span multiple metabolic pathways: TCA cycle (succinate dehydrogenase — complex II of ETC); β-oxidation (acyl-CoA dehydrogenase); purine catabolism (xanthine oxidase → uric acid); antioxidant defense (glutathione reductase regenerates GSH using NADPH); amino acid catabolism (glycine cleavage system, D-amino acid oxidase); and oxidative decarboxylation complexes (PDC and α-KGDH, where FAD is in the dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase subunit).

questions.text: What are the manifestations of riboflavin deficiency?
questions.answer: Glossitis, cheilosis, angular stomatitis, and corneal vascularization.
questions.explanation: Riboflavin deficiency (ariboflavinosis) predominantly affects rapidly proliferating epithelial tissues: (1) Glossitis — inflamed, magenta-colored tongue; (2) Cheilosis — dry, cracked lips; (3) Angular stomatitis (angular cheilitis) — fissures at the corners of the mouth; (4) Corneal vascularization (interstitial keratitis) — neovascularization of the cornea causing photophobia; (5) Seborrheic dermatitis around the nose and scrotum. Isolated riboflavin deficiency is rare; it usually accompanies other B-vitamin deficiencies.

questions.text: What are the dietary sources of riboflavin?
questions.answer: Liver, dried yeast, eggs, and milk.
questions.explanation: Riboflavin is widely distributed in animal and plant foods. The richest sources are organ meats (liver, kidney), dairy products (milk, yogurt, cheese), eggs, and yeast. Green leafy vegetables and whole grains provide smaller amounts. Riboflavin is sensitive to UV light — milk stored in clear bottles loses significant riboflavin content due to photodegradation. Unlike thiamine, riboflavin is relatively heat-stable.

questions.text: What is the daily requirement of riboflavin?
questions.answer: 1.5 mg/day.
questions.explanation: The RDA for riboflavin in adults is 1.1–1.3 mg/day, proportional to energy expenditure and protein intake. Requirements increase during pregnancy (1.4 mg/day), lactation (1.6 mg/day), and periods of rapid growth. Since riboflavin is water-soluble and excreted in urine, excess intake is non-toxic. Bright yellow fluorescent urine after riboflavin supplementation is normal and harmless.

questions.text: What are the coenzymes derived from niacin?
questions.answer: NAD⁺ (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) and NADP⁺ (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate).
questions.explanation: Niacin (vitamin B₃) encompasses nicotinic acid and nicotinamide. Both are converted to NAD⁺ via the Preiss-Handler pathway or salvage pathway. NAD⁺ is phosphorylated to NADP⁺ by NAD⁺ kinase. These dinucleotides function as diffusible electron carriers — unlike FAD/FMN — accepting a hydride ion (H⁻, equivalent to 2e⁻ + H⁺) at the nicotinamide ring to form NADH and NADPH, respectively.

questions.text: Name some important NAD⁺-dependent enzymes.
questions.answer: Lactate dehydrogenase, glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, pyruvate dehydrogenase, β-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase, and mitochondrial isocitrate dehydrogenase.
questions.explanation: NAD⁺ is the primary electron acceptor in catabolic (energy-releasing) pathways: glycolysis (G3PDH — step 6), TCA cycle (isocitrate dehydrogenase, α-KGDH, malate dehydrogenase), β-oxidation (β-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase), and anaerobic metabolism (lactate dehydrogenase — regenerates NAD⁺ from NADH under hypoxic conditions). Each NADH generated feeds electrons into complex I of the ETC, yielding approximately 2.5 ATP.

questions.text: What is the importance of niacin?
questions.answer: (1) Niacin enters the structure of NAD⁺ and NADP⁺, which act as hydrogen (electron) carriers in metabolism. (2) Niacin lowers plasma cholesterol.
questions.explanation: Pharmacological doses of nicotinic acid (niacin, 1–3 g/day) have potent lipid-lowering effects: reduces VLDL synthesis and secretion from the liver (by inhibiting diacylglycerol acyltransferase and decreasing FFA mobilization from adipose tissue), lowers LDL-cholesterol, and raises HDL-cholesterol (by reducing HDL apoA-I catabolism). This makes niacin one of the most effective agents for raising HDL. The main side effect is prostaglandin-mediated cutaneous flushing, reduced by aspirin pretreatment.

questions.text: Name the NADPH-generating reactions.
questions.answer: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase, malic enzyme, and cytosolic isocitrate dehydrogenase.
questions.explanation: NADPH is the major reductant for anabolic reactions and antioxidant defense: (1) Pentose phosphate pathway (PPP): G6PD and 6-PGD are the primary NADPH sources, especially in RBCs; (2) Malic enzyme: converts malate → pyruvate + NADPH in the cytosol (lipogenesis support); (3) Cytosolic isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH1): generates NADPH for antioxidant defense. NADPH is essential for fatty acid synthesis, cholesterol synthesis, glutathione reduction (GPx cycle), and cytochrome P450 reactions.

questions.text: What are the important NADPH-utilizing reactions?
questions.answer: β-Ketoacyl-CoA reductase, α,β-unsaturated acyl-CoA reductase, HMG-CoA reductase, methemoglobin reductase, dihydrofolate reductase, and phenylalanine hydroxylase.
questions.explanation: NADPH drives reductive biosynthesis and protective reactions: (1) Fatty acid synthesis (FAS complex — reductive steps); (2) Cholesterol synthesis (HMG-CoA reductase — rate-limiting step, target of statins); (3) Methemoglobin reduction (NADPH-methemoglobin reductase keeps hemoglobin functional); (4) Folate activation (DHFR reduces dihydrofolate → tetrahydrofolate); (5) Phenylalanine hydroxylase (requires tetrahydrobiopterin regenerated by DHPR using NADPH); (6) Glutathione regeneration (glutathione reductase — antioxidant defense).

questions.text: Pellagra is seen in the deficiency of which vitamin?
questions.answer: Niacin (Vitamin B₃).
questions.explanation: Pellagra (Italian: 'rough skin') is the classic niacin deficiency disease. It is historically associated with maize (corn)-based diets, as corn is low in both niacin and tryptophan (its precursor), and the niacin present is in a bound, bioavailable form (niacytin) that is not absorbed unless treated with alkali (nixtamalization). The disease was epidemic in the American South and parts of Europe in the early 20th century.

questions.text: What are the features of pellagra?
questions.answer: The 3 Ds: Dermatitis, Diarrhea, and Dementia.
questions.explanation: Pellagra's classic triad (sometimes 4 Ds including Death if untreated): (1) Dermatitis — photosensitive, symmetric rash on sun-exposed areas (Casal's necklace around the neck); hyperpigmented, scaling lesions; (2) Diarrhea — atrophic gastritis, glossitis, stomatitis, bloody diarrhea due to mucosal atrophy; (3) Dementia — anxiety, depression, confusion, hallucinations, and eventually dementia from impaired NAD⁺-dependent neuronal energy metabolism. Treatment: oral niacin supplementation with prompt clinical improvement.

questions.text: What is the precursor of niacin?
questions.answer: Tryptophan.
questions.explanation: Tryptophan is an essential amino acid that can be converted to niacin via the kynurenine pathway. The key enzyme is kynurenine hydroxylase, requiring FAD (riboflavin). The final step is conversion of quinolinic acid to nicotinic acid mononucleotide (NaMN), entering the NAD⁺ synthesis pathway. This endogenous synthesis is vitamin B₆-dependent (for kynureninase) and provides only a portion of niacin needs.

questions.text: How much tryptophan gives rise to how much niacin?
questions.answer: Approximately 60 mg of tryptophan yields 1 mg of niacin.
questions.explanation: The 60:1 conversion ratio (60 mg Trp → 1 mg niacin) is the basis for expressing dietary niacin in 'niacin equivalents' (NE): 1 NE = 1 mg niacin = 60 mg tryptophan. This conversion efficiency is reduced in vitamin B₆ deficiency (kynureninase requires PLP), riboflavin deficiency, and in conditions of high tryptophan demand (carcinoid syndrome, Hartnup disease), all of which can precipitate pellagra.

questions.text: Tryptophan is deficient in which foodstuffs?
questions.answer: Maize (corn) and sorghum.
questions.explanation: Maize (corn) protein (zein) is severely deficient in both tryptophan and lysine, and most of its niacin is bound as niacytin (nicotinic acid esterified to polysaccharides), which is not bioavailable without alkaline treatment. Populations dependent on corn as a staple (without nixtamalization) are at high risk for pellagra. The traditional Mesoamerican practice of treating corn with lime water (nixtamalization) releases bound niacin and significantly increases bioavailability.

questions.text: Which conditions lead to symptoms of pellagra?
questions.answer: Low tryptophan content in diet, niacin deficiency, Vitamin B₆ deficiency, Hartnup disease, and carcinoid syndrome.
questions.explanation: Pellagra-like symptoms arise whenever the niacin/tryptophan supply or metabolism is compromised: (1) Dietary niacin/tryptophan deficiency (maize-based diets); (2) B₆ deficiency — impairs kynureninase (PLP-dependent), reducing tryptophan → niacin conversion; (3) Hartnup disease — autosomal recessive defect in neutral amino acid transporter (SLC6A19), causing intestinal and renal tryptophan wasting; (4) Carcinoid syndrome — tumor diverts tryptophan to serotonin synthesis, reducing niacin production.

questions.text: Which drugs lead to symptoms of pellagra?
questions.answer: Isoniazid (INH) therapy.
questions.explanation: Isoniazid (isonicotinic acid hydrazide) — a first-line antituberculosis drug — is a structural analogue of pyridoxine that forms a hydrazone complex with pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), inhibiting PLP-dependent enzymes. Since PLP is required by kynureninase in the tryptophan → niacin pathway, INH effectively blocks endogenous niacin synthesis. Prophylactic pyridoxine (Vitamin B₆) supplementation is routinely co-administered with INH to prevent peripheral neuropathy and pellagra-like symptoms.

questions.text: What are the dietary sources of niacin?
questions.answer: Whole grain cereals, milk, meat, liver, and yeast. Niacin can also be synthesized endogenously from the amino acid tryptophan.
questions.explanation: Niacin is widely distributed in both animal and plant foods. Rich sources include: organ meats (liver), poultry, fish, peanuts, and whole grains. Milk and eggs contain little preformed niacin but are good tryptophan sources. Niacin from animal sources is more bioavailable than from plant sources. Instant coffee is a surprisingly significant source of niacin.

questions.text: What is the daily requirement of niacin?
questions.answer: 20 mg/day (niacin equivalents).
questions.explanation: The RDA for niacin is 14–16 mg NE/day for adults (higher for men due to greater muscle mass and energy expenditure). Pharmacological doses (1000–3000 mg/day of nicotinic acid) are used for dyslipidemia but require medical supervision due to side effects including flushing, hepatotoxicity (with extended-release forms), and hyperglycemia.

questions.text: Which vitamin is required for transamination reactions?
questions.answer: Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) — the active coenzyme form of Vitamin B₆.
questions.explanation: PLP (pyridoxal-5'-phosphate) is the universal coenzyme for amino acid metabolism. In transamination, PLP forms a Schiff base (aldimine) with the amino group of the amino acid substrate. The amino group is transferred to PLP, converting it to pyridoxamine phosphate (PMP), which then transfers the amino group to an α-keto acid acceptor, regenerating PLP. This mechanism is used by all aminotransferases (transaminases).

questions.text: What reactions require pyridoxal phosphate (PLP)?
questions.answer: Transamination of amino acids, decarboxylation of amino acids, and heme synthesis.
questions.explanation: PLP is the most versatile coenzyme in amino acid metabolism, required for: (1) Transamination — AST, ALT (diagnostically important liver enzymes); (2) Decarboxylation — synthesis of neurotransmitters, biogenic amines; (3) Heme synthesis — δ-aminolevulinate (ALA) synthase (rate-limiting enzyme); (4) Tryptophan catabolism (kynureninase); (5) Cystathionine β-synthase and cystathionase (transsulfuration pathway); (6) Glycogen phosphorylase (PLP here acts structurally, not as a cofactor); (7) Serine hydroxymethyltransferase.

questions.text: Give examples of transamination reactions.
questions.answer: Aspartate transaminase (AST): aspartate + α-ketoglutarate → oxaloacetate + glutamate. Alanine transaminase (ALT): alanine + α-ketoglutarate → pyruvate + glutamate.
questions.explanation: Transamination reactions (aminotransferases) are reversible and central to amino acid metabolism and gluconeogenesis. AST (GOT) and ALT (GPT) are clinically important: elevated serum levels indicate hepatocellular damage (ALT is more liver-specific). Both require PLP and use α-ketoglutarate as the amino group acceptor, funneling nitrogen toward glutamate for subsequent urea cycle entry or glutamine synthesis.

questions.text: Give examples of decarboxylation reactions requiring PLP.
questions.answer: Glutamate → GABA; Histidine → Histamine; 5-hydroxytryptophan → Serotonin; Cysteine → Taurine; Serine → Ethanolamine.
questions.explanation: PLP-dependent decarboxylases produce key biologically active amines and neurotransmitters: (1) Glutamate decarboxylase → GABA (major inhibitory CNS neurotransmitter; deficiency causes convulsions); (2) Histidine decarboxylase → Histamine (allergy mediator); (3) DOPA decarboxylase (aromatic amino acid decarboxylase) → dopamine, serotonin (from 5-HTP); (4) Cysteine sulfinase pathway → taurine (bile acid conjugation, antioxidant); (5) Serine decarboxylase → ethanolamine (phospholipid synthesis).

questions.text: What vitamins are important for hydrogen carriage?
questions.answer: Vitamin B₂ (riboflavin — as FMN/FAD), nicotinic acid (as NAD⁺/NADP⁺), and lipoic acid. Vitamin C in its oxidized form may also have a role.
questions.explanation: Biological oxidation involves sequential transfer of hydrogen atoms (electrons + protons): NAD⁺/NADP⁺ (niacin-derived) accept hydride ions (2e⁻ + H⁺) from dehydrogenase reactions; FAD/FMN (riboflavin-derived) accept two electrons and two protons from flavoprotein reactions; Lipoic acid (as dihydrolipoamide) transfers electrons and acetyl groups in α-keto acid dehydrogenase complexes; Vitamin C (ascorbate/dehydroascorbate redox couple) participates in electron transfer reactions including collagen hydroxylation.

questions.text: What are the manifestations of pyridoxal (B₆) deficiency?
questions.answer: Pellagra-like rash, infantile convulsions, anemia, increased cancer risk (breast), and disturbances in amino acid metabolism.
questions.explanation: B₆ deficiency manifestations reflect its widespread role in amino acid metabolism: (1) Pellagra-like rash — impaired tryptophan → niacin conversion; (2) Infantile convulsions — deficient GABA synthesis (glutamate decarboxylase requires PLP); (3) Sideroblastic anemia — impaired ALA synthase → deficient heme; (4) Hyperhomocysteinemia — impaired transsulfuration (CBS and cystathionase require PLP) → cardiovascular risk; (5) Peripheral neuropathy; (6) Glossitis, seborrheic dermatitis.

questions.text: What is the reason for mental retardation in pyridoxal deficiency?
questions.answer: Disturbances in amino acid metabolism affecting neurotransmitter synthesis and brain development.
questions.explanation: PLP deficiency impairs synthesis of neurotransmitters derived from amino acids: reduced GABA (from glutamate), serotonin (from 5-HTP), dopamine (from DOPA), and norepinephrine. In neonates and infants, these deficiencies during critical periods of brain development can cause permanent intellectual disability. Pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy (ALDH7A1 mutations causing PLP inactivation) is a rare genetic condition where high-dose B₆ is lifesaving.

questions.text: What is the reason for infantile convulsions in pyridoxal deficiency?
questions.answer: PLP is required for GABA synthesis (glutamate decarboxylase). Deficiency leads to reduced GABA levels, causing neuronal hyperexcitability and convulsions.
questions.explanation: GABA (γ-aminobutyric acid) is the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS, synthesized by PLP-dependent glutamate decarboxylase (GAD). In pyridoxal deficiency, GAD activity falls, GABA levels drop, and the inhibitory tone on neuronal firing is lost, resulting in hyperexcitability and seizures. This explains why neonates born to mothers on isoniazid (INH) therapy or with pyridoxine dependency may present with intractable seizures responsive to IV pyridoxine.

questions.text: What is the reason for pellagra-like disease in pyridoxal deficiency?
questions.answer: Because PLP is needed for the conversion of tryptophan to niacin (kynureninase requires PLP). Deficiency reduces niacin synthesis.
questions.explanation: The kynurenine pathway converts tryptophan to niacin through multiple PLP-dependent steps, particularly kynureninase (kynurenine aminohydrolase). In B₆ deficiency, this enzyme is impaired, causing: (1) Accumulation of xanthurenic acid and kynurenine (xanthurenic acid excretion test is a diagnostic test for B₆ deficiency); (2) Reduced niacin synthesis → pellagra-like dermatitis and neurological symptoms.

questions.text: Can you give an example of one vitamin deficiency leading to another vitamin deficiency?
questions.answer: Vitamin B₆ deficiency leads to niacin deficiency (manifested as pellagra), because PLP is required for the conversion of tryptophan to niacin.
questions.explanation: This illustrates metabolic interdependence between B vitamins: PLP-dependent kynureninase is essential for the tryptophan → niacin pathway. Without adequate B₆, endogenous niacin synthesis is impaired, and if dietary niacin is also marginal, pellagra develops. Similarly, B₁₂ deficiency leads to functional folate deficiency (methyl folate trap), and riboflavin deficiency impairs the tryptophan → niacin conversion (kynurenine hydroxylase is FAD-dependent).

questions.text: What is the reason for anemia in pyridoxal deficiency?
questions.answer: B₆ is required for ALA synthase, the key enzyme in heme synthesis. Deficiency leads to deficient heme and hemoglobin formation, producing hypochromic microcytic (sideroblastic) anemia.
questions.explanation: ALA synthase (δ-aminolevulinate synthase) catalyzes the rate-limiting step of heme biosynthesis: succinyl-CoA + glycine → δ-ALA (requires PLP). In B₆ deficiency, ALA synthase activity falls → heme synthesis is impaired → hemoglobin production decreases. Iron accumulates in mitochondria of developing erythrocytes (ringed sideroblasts on bone marrow Prussian blue stain), producing sideroblastic anemia — characterized by hypochromic, microcytic red cells with elevated serum iron and ferritin.

questions.text: What drugs cause pyridoxal deficiency?
questions.answer: Isoniazid (INH), oral contraceptives, and ethanol (converted to acetaldehyde, which inactivates PLP).
questions.explanation: Drug-induced B₆ deficiency mechanisms: (1) Isoniazid — forms hydrazone adduct with PLP, inactivating it; also inhibits pyridoxal kinase; (2) Oral contraceptives (estrogens) — increase tryptophan catabolism, increasing PLP demand, and may alter B₆ metabolism; (3) Ethanol → acetaldehyde (by alcohol dehydrogenase) → acetaldehyde displaces PLP from its binding proteins → PLP undergoes increased hydrolysis by phosphatase; (4) Penicillamine — forms stable complex with PLP; (5) Hydralazine and cycloserine — also inactivate PLP.

questions.text: What are the dietary sources of pyridoxal phosphate (Vitamin B₆)?
questions.answer: Yeast, wheat, cereals, egg yolk, liver, meat, milk, fish, and green leafy vegetables.
questions.explanation: Vitamin B₆ is widely distributed in both plant and animal foods. The richest sources include: poultry, fish (tuna, salmon), organ meats (liver), potatoes, bananas, fortified cereals, and legumes. Animal sources contain predominantly PLP and PMP (readily absorbed), while plant sources contain pyridoxine-5'-glucoside (lower bioavailability). Vitamin B₆ is heat-labile and destroyed by food processing and cooking.

questions.text: What is the daily requirement of pyridoxal phosphate (Vitamin B₆)?
questions.answer: 2 mg/day.
questions.explanation: The RDA for B₆ in adults is 1.3–1.7 mg/day, increasing with age and protein intake (B₆ requirement is proportional to protein consumption). The tolerable upper limit is 100 mg/day — chronic high-dose supplementation (>200 mg/day) causes sensory neuropathy (ataxia and peripheral nerve damage). Unlike most water-soluble vitamins, B₆ toxicity has been well-documented with supplement abuse.

questions.text: Enumerate vitamins containing a pyridine ring.
questions.answer: Nicotinic acid (niacin/Vitamin B₃) and Vitamin B₆ (pyridoxine/pyridoxal phosphate).
questions.explanation: The pyridine ring (a six-membered aromatic ring with one nitrogen) is the core structure of: (1) Niacin (nicotinic acid) — the pyridine-3-carboxylic acid; the nicotinamide ring in NAD⁺ and NADP⁺ is a pyridinium (quaternary nitrogen) that accepts a hydride ion during reduction; (2) Pyridoxine/pyridoxal/pyridoxamine (Vitamin B₆) — all three are 2-methyl-3-hydroxypyridine derivatives substituted at position 4 with a hydroxymethyl, aldehyde, or aminomethyl group, respectively.

questions.text: What vitamins are important for decarboxylation reactions?
questions.answer: Vitamin B₁ (thiamine — as TPP) and Vitamin B₆ (pyridoxal phosphate).
questions.explanation: Decarboxylation in biochemistry involves two distinct types: (1) Oxidative decarboxylation of α-keto acids (pyruvate, α-ketoglutarate) — requires TPP (B₁), lipoic acid, FAD (B₂), NAD⁺ (B₃), and CoA (B₅) as components of multienzyme complexes; (2) Amino acid decarboxylation (production of biogenic amines and neurotransmitters) — requires PLP (B₆) exclusively. Biotin also catalyzes carboxylation reactions (CO₂ fixation) but these are the reverse process.

questions.text: What is the importance of pantothenic acid (Vitamin B₅)?
questions.answer: Pantothenic acid is a structural component of Coenzyme A (CoA) and acyl carrier protein (ACP).
questions.explanation: Pantothenic acid (from Greek 'pantos' = everywhere) is ubiquitous in foods and isolated deficiency is extremely rare. It is incorporated into CoA via phosphopantetheine, which consists of β-mercaptoethylamine + pantothenate + phosphate. The thiol (–SH) group of CoA is the reactive site that forms high-energy thioester bonds with acyl groups. ACP, used in fatty acid synthesis, contains a 4'-phosphopantetheine prosthetic group that carries acyl intermediates between enzyme active sites in the FAS complex.

questions.text: What is the coenzyme form of pantothenic acid?
questions.answer: Coenzyme A (CoA).
questions.explanation: CoA (coenzyme A) structure: adenosine-3',5'-bisphosphate + pantothenic acid + β-mercaptoethylamine, linked via a phosphoanhydride and amide bonds. The functional group is the free thiol (–SH) at the end of the pantetheine arm, which forms thioester bonds (R–CO–S–CoA) with acyl groups. Acyl-CoA thioesters have high group-transfer potential, making CoA an essential activating agent for acyl group transfer in fatty acid metabolism, TCA cycle, and cholesterol synthesis.

questions.text: What is the function of CoA?
questions.answer: Coenzyme A acts in the transfer of acyl groups — e.g., acetyl-CoA, succinyl-CoA, malonyl-CoA, and other carboxylic acid thioesters.
questions.explanation: CoA functions as a universal acyl group carrier and activator. Key acyl-CoA species and their metabolic roles: (1) Acetyl-CoA — entry into TCA cycle, fatty acid synthesis, ketone body synthesis, cholesterol synthesis; (2) Succinyl-CoA — heme synthesis, TCA cycle; (3) Malonyl-CoA — fatty acid chain elongation (FAS substrate), inhibitor of CPT-1 (prevents β-oxidation during lipogenesis); (4) Fatty acyl-CoA — β-oxidation; (5) Acetoacetyl-CoA — ketogenesis and cholesterol synthesis.

questions.text: What is the importance of acetyl-CoA?
questions.answer: Acetyl-CoA is a central metabolic intermediate in carbohydrate, lipid, and protein metabolism.
questions.explanation: Acetyl-CoA is the pivotal metabolic hub connecting all three macronutrient pathways: From carbohydrates — pyruvate dehydrogenase converts pyruvate (glycolysis product) to acetyl-CoA; From fats — β-oxidation of fatty acids produces acetyl-CoA; From proteins — carbon skeletons of ketogenic amino acids are degraded to acetyl-CoA. Acetyl-CoA then enters: TCA cycle (energy production), fatty acid synthesis (lipogenesis), ketogenesis, cholesterol/steroid synthesis, and acetylcholine synthesis.

questions.text: What is the importance of ACP (acyl carrier protein)?
questions.answer: ACP acts as an acyl carrier during the reactions of the extra-mitochondrial (cytosolic) pathway for fatty acid synthesis.
questions.explanation: ACP is a small protein (~8.8 kDa in bacteria; a domain within the multifunctional FAS complex in mammals) that carries acyl intermediates via its 4'-phosphopantetheine prosthetic group during de novo fatty acid synthesis. The acyl chain is attached as a thioester to the terminal –SH of the phosphopantetheine arm. ACP shuttles the growing acyl chain between the seven catalytic domains of the mammalian FAS complex (a homodimer of 250 kDa subunits), enabling the cyclic elongation process from acetyl-CoA and malonyl-CoA to palmitate (C16:0).

questions.text: What is the function of biotin (Vitamin B₇)?
questions.answer: CO₂ fixation in carboxylation reactions.
questions.explanation: Biotin serves as a covalently bound coenzyme (attached via an amide bond to a lysine residue of the apoenzyme — forming biocytin) for all carboxylase enzymes. It acts as a CO₂ carrier: in an ATP-dependent first step, bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) is attached to the N1' of biotin's ureido ring, forming carboxybiotin; in the second step, the activated CO₂ is transferred to the substrate. This two-step mechanism allows fixation of one carbon unit (CO₂) into organic molecules.

questions.text: Name some reactions dependent on biotin.
questions.answer: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase, propionyl-CoA carboxylase, and pyruvate carboxylase.
questions.explanation: Biotin-dependent carboxylases and their metabolic roles: (1) Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) — converts acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA; rate-limiting step in fatty acid synthesis; regulated by citrate (activator) and palmitoyl-CoA (inhibitor); (2) Pyruvate carboxylase — converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate; key anaplerotic reaction replenishing TCA cycle intermediates; essential for gluconeogenesis; (3) Propionyl-CoA carboxylase — converts propionyl-CoA to methylmalonyl-CoA; part of odd-chain fatty acid and branched-chain amino acid catabolism. Also: β-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase (leucine catabolism).

questions.text: What is the antagonist for biotin?
questions.answer: Avidin.
questions.explanation: Avidin is a glycoprotein found in raw egg white that binds biotin with extraordinary affinity (Kd ≈ 10⁻¹⁵ M — one of the strongest non-covalent interactions in biology), preventing its intestinal absorption. Cooking denatures avidin, abolishing its biotin-binding capacity — explaining why cooked eggs do not cause biotin deficiency but consuming large quantities of raw egg whites does. Streptavidin (from Streptomyces avidinii) has similar biotin-binding properties and is widely used in biotechnology and diagnostic assays.

questions.text: What vitamins are important for CO₂ fixation?
questions.answer: Biotin is the only vitamin used for CO₂ fixation.
questions.explanation: All mammalian CO₂-fixing (carboxylation) reactions use biotin as the CO₂ carrier coenzyme. This distinguishes biotin from other B vitamins: whereas TPP (B₁) and PLP (B₆) are involved in decarboxylation (removing CO₂), biotin uniquely performs the reverse — adding CO₂ to substrates in ATP-dependent carboxylation reactions. This role is essential for fatty acid synthesis, gluconeogenesis, and propionate metabolism.

questions.text: What are the sources of folic acid?
questions.answer: The major source is leafy vegetables. Folic acid is also present in yeast, liver, beans, and whole grain cereals.
questions.explanation: The name 'folic acid' derives from the Latin 'folium' (leaf), reflecting its abundance in green leafy vegetables (spinach, asparagus, broccoli). Natural folates in food are predominantly in the reduced polyglutamate form (tetrahydrofolate polyglutamates), which must be hydrolyzed to monoglutamate by intestinal conjugase (γ-glutamyl hydrolase) before absorption. Synthetic folic acid (in supplements and fortified foods) is the oxidized monoglutamate form, which is more stable and bioavailable than food folates.

questions.text: What is the chemical nature of folic acid?
questions.answer: Pteroyl glutamic acid — composed of pteridine + PABA (para-aminobenzoic acid) + glutamic acid.
questions.explanation: Folic acid (pteroylmonoglutamic acid) structure: (1) Pteridine ring — a bicyclic aromatic ring system (pyrimidine fused with pyrazine); (2) Para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) — linked to pteridine via a methylene bridge; (3) Glutamic acid — linked to PABA via a peptide bond. Natural folates contain 5–8 additional glutamate residues (polyglutamate tail) added by folylpolyglutamate synthetase, which increases intracellular retention and enzymatic affinity. The pteridine ring undergoes two reduction steps (by dihydrofolate reductase, DHFR) to yield tetrahydrofolate (THF/H₄folate) — the active coenzyme form.

questions.text: What is PABA?
questions.answer: Para-aminobenzoic acid — a structural component of folic acid.
questions.explanation: PABA is an intermediate in folate biosynthesis in bacteria and plants. Bacteria synthesize folate de novo from pteridine + PABA + glutamate, a pathway absent in mammals (who must obtain folate from diet). Sulfonamide antibiotics exploit this difference: they are structural analogues of PABA that competitively inhibit dihydropteroate synthase (the bacterial enzyme that incorporates PABA into folate), selectively blocking bacterial folate synthesis without affecting mammalian cells.

questions.text: What is the coenzyme form of folic acid?
questions.answer: Tetrahydrofolic acid (THFA / H₄folate).
questions.explanation: Folic acid must be reduced twice to its active coenzyme form: Folic acid → dihydrofolate (DHF, H₂folate) → tetrahydrofolate (THF, H₄folate). Both steps are catalyzed by dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), which uses NADPH as the reductant. The pteridine ring is reduced at N5-N6 and N7-N8 positions. THF is the actual one-carbon carrier, with one-carbon units attached at N5, N10, or bridging N5-N10 positions. This is why DHFR inhibitors (methotrexate, trimethoprim) block folate function even when dietary folate is adequate.

questions.text: What is the main function of folic acid?
questions.answer: Tetrahydrofolic acid (THFA) is the carrier of one-carbon units in metabolic reactions.
questions.explanation: THF functions as a one-carbon unit carrier analogous to how CoA carries acyl groups. The one-carbon units (at various oxidation states) are attached to N5 or N10 (or bridging both) of THF: N5-methyl-THF carries the methyl group; N5,N10-methylene-THF carries the methylene group; N5,N10-methenyl-THF carries the methenyl group; N10-formyl-THF carries the formyl group. These one-carbon-loaded THF species donate their carbon units to biosynthetic reactions for purines, thymidylate, methionine, and serine.

questions.text: Give examples of one-carbon units.
questions.answer: Methyl (–CH₃), methylene (–CH₂–), methenyl (–CH=), formyl (–CHO), and formimino (–CH=NH) groups.
questions.explanation: One-carbon units differ in their oxidation state (most oxidized to most reduced): Formyl (–CHO, oxidation state +2) → Methenyl (–CH=, +1) → Methylene (–CH₂–, 0) → Methyl (–CH₃, –2). Each form is carried by THF at a specific nitrogen position and is interconvertible by oxidoreductases. The methyl group on N5-methyl-THF is the most reduced form and can only be released via methionine synthase (B₁₂-dependent) — explaining the methyl folate trap in B₁₂ deficiency.

questions.text: What are the sources of one-carbon moieties (groups)?
questions.answer: β-carbon of serine, α-carbon of glycine, tryptophan, and histidine.
questions.explanation: Major one-carbon donors to THF: (1) Serine (most important) — serine hydroxymethyltransferase (SHMT, PLP-dependent) transfers the β-carbon of serine to THF → N5,N10-methylene-THF + glycine; (2) Glycine — the glycine cleavage system (glycine decarboxylase complex) releases C2 of glycine as N5,N10-methylene-THF; (3) Tryptophan — via formate through the kynurenine pathway; (4) Histidine — formiminoglutamate (FIGLU) donates formimino group to THF → N5-formimino-THF (used in the FIGLU excretion test for folate deficiency).

questions.text: What are the fates of one-carbon moieties (groups)?
questions.answer: Synthesis of glycine; conversion of glycine to serine; conversion of homocysteine to methionine; conversion of uracil to thymine (dUMP → dTMP); provides C2 and C8 of purines.
questions.explanation: One-carbon unit utilization by THF species: (1) N5,N10-methylene-THF → thymidylate synthase → dTMP from dUMP (DNA synthesis — rate-limiting step targeted by 5-fluorouracil); (2) N10-formyl-THF → provides C2 and C8 of the purine ring (IMP synthesis); (3) N5-methyl-THF → methionine synthase (B₁₂-dependent) → methionine from homocysteine; (4) N5,N10-methylene-THF → SHMT (reverse) → serine from glycine. Impairment of any of these by folate or B₁₂ deficiency disrupts nucleotide synthesis and cell division.

questions.text: On which atoms of H₄folate are one-carbon units carried?
questions.answer: On N5 or N10 or both (bridging N5–N10).
questions.explanation: The N5 and N10 positions of the pteridine ring of THF are the attachment sites for one-carbon units: N5 only: N5-methyl-THF (carries –CH₃); N5-formimino-THF (carries –CH=NH). N10 only: N10-formyl-THF (carries –CHO). N5–N10 bridge: N5,N10-methylene-THF (carries –CH₂–); N5,N10-methenyl-THF (carries –CH=). The interconversion between these forms is catalyzed by specific oxidoreductases and is linked to the NADP⁺/NADPH redox couple.

questions.text: What are the causes of folate deficiency?
questions.answer: Pregnancy, defective absorption, anticonvulsant drugs, hemolytic anemias, and dietary deficiency.
questions.explanation: Causes of folate deficiency: (1) Increased demand — pregnancy (neural tube closure requires folate; periconceptional supplementation prevents NTDs), hemolytic anemias (rapid erythrocyte turnover), rapid cell growth; (2) Decreased intake — poor diet, alcoholism, elderly; (3) Malabsorption — celiac disease, Crohn's, tropical sprue; (4) Drug interference — methotrexate and trimethoprim (DHFR inhibitors), anticonvulsants (phenytoin impairs folate absorption and increases catabolism), oral contraceptives; (5) Liver disease (impaired storage and metabolism).

questions.text: What is the major manifestation of folic acid deficiency?
questions.answer: Macrocytic (megaloblastic) anemia.
questions.explanation: Folate deficiency impairs DNA synthesis (specifically thymidylate and purine synthesis) in rapidly dividing cells. In hematopoietic precursors, defective DNA replication allows cytoplasmic growth to continue unchecked (RNA and protein synthesis are unaffected), producing abnormally large cells (megaloblasts). The resulting peripheral blood picture shows macrocytic (large) red blood cells with hypersegmented neutrophils (>5 lobes). Unlike B₁₂ deficiency, folate deficiency alone does not cause neurological manifestations.

questions.text: What are the laboratory findings in folic acid deficiency?
questions.answer: (1) Peripheral blood shows macrocytic anemia. (2) Decreased serum folic acid level. (3) Increased FIGLU excretion in urine, especially after histidine loading.
questions.explanation: Laboratory diagnosis of folate deficiency: (1) CBC: macrocytic anemia (MCV >100 fL), hypersegmented neutrophils (Papppenheimer bodies); (2) Serum folate <3 ng/mL (reflects recent intake); RBC folate <140 ng/mL (reflects tissue stores — more reliable); (3) Elevated plasma homocysteine (folate needed for homocysteine → methionine conversion); (4) FIGLU excretion test: oral histidine load → FIGLU accumulates if THF is insufficient → elevated urinary FIGLU (normal: <17 mg/day); (5) Normal methylmalonic acid (distinguishes from B₁₂ deficiency).

questions.text: What is FIGlu?
questions.answer: Formiminoglutamate — an intermediate in histidine catabolism that donates its formimino group to tetrahydrofolate, leaving glutamate which is then converted to α-ketoglutarate.
questions.explanation: FIGLU (N-formiminoglutamate) is formed in the catabolism of histidine: histidine → urocanate → 4-imidazolone-5-propionate → FIGLU → glutamate + formimino-THF (via glutamate formiminotransferase). In folate deficiency, THF is unavailable to accept the formimino group, causing FIGLU to accumulate and spill into urine. The FIGLU excretion test exploits this: a histidine load (5–20 g) is given, and a 24-hour urine collection measures FIGLU. Elevated excretion indicates folate deficiency.

questions.text: What is the FIGlu excretion test?
questions.answer: In folate deficiency, FIGLU excretion in urine is increased. This is a useful diagnostic test for folic acid deficiency.
questions.explanation: The FIGLU excretion test procedure: (1) Administer an oral histidine load (15–20 g); (2) Collect urine for 8–24 hours; (3) Measure FIGLU by colorimetric or chromatographic methods. Normal individuals efficiently transfer the formimino group from FIGLU to THF (via formiminotransferase), excreting minimal FIGLU (<17 mg/24h). In folate deficiency, THF is insufficient, FIGLU accumulates in plasma and spills into urine (>35 mg/24h). Also elevated in B₁₂ deficiency (methyl folate trap reduces available THF).

questions.text: What is the daily requirement of folic acid?
questions.answer: 200 μg/day. In pregnancy, the requirement increases to 400 μg/day.
questions.explanation: Folate requirements: Adults: 400 μg dietary folate equivalents (DFE)/day; Pregnancy: 600 μg DFE/day (periconceptional supplementation of 400 μg synthetic folic acid/day reduces neural tube defect risk by 50–70%); Lactation: 500 μg DFE/day. The DFE accounts for the higher bioavailability of synthetic folic acid (in supplements/fortified foods) vs. natural food folates: 1 DFE = 1 μg food folate = 0.6 μg synthetic folic acid from food = 0.5 μg synthetic folic acid as supplement.

questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of sulphonamides?
questions.answer: Sulfonamides are structural analogues of PABA. They competitively inhibit the bacterial enzyme that incorporates PABA into folic acid (dihydropteroate synthase), blocking bacterial folate synthesis.
questions.explanation: Sulfonamides (e.g., sulfamethoxazole) selectively target bacterial folate synthesis because: (1) Bacteria must synthesize their own folate (cannot absorb preformed folate); (2) Mammals obtain folate from diet and lack dihydropteroate synthase. Sulfonamides are bacteriostatic. They are often combined with trimethoprim (co-trimoxazole = sulfamethoxazole + trimethoprim), which inhibits bacterial DHFR — creating sequential blockade of two steps in the folate pathway, producing synergistic bactericidal activity.

questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of trimethoprim?
questions.answer: Trimethoprim is a bactericidal agent. It inhibits folate reductase (dihydrofolate reductase — DHFR), reducing the formation of tetrahydrofolic acid (THFA).
questions.explanation: Trimethoprim selectively inhibits bacterial DHFR with ~50,000-fold greater affinity than mammalian DHFR, making it selectively toxic to bacteria. It binds competitively to the DHFR active site, blocking reduction of DHF → THF. This depletes active THF, halting bacterial nucleotide synthesis and cell division. When combined with sulfamethoxazole (co-trimoxazole), the sequential double blockade is bactericidal and reduces the likelihood of resistance development.

questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of methotrexate?
questions.answer: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) and is a powerful anticancer drug.
questions.explanation: Methotrexate (MTX) is a folate antimetabolite that binds DHFR with 1000-fold greater affinity than dihydrofolate, acting as a tight-binding inhibitor. It depletes THF, blocking: (1) Thymidylate synthesis (dUMP → dTMP via thymidylate synthase) — 'thymineless death'; (2) Purine synthesis (C2 and C8). Rapidly dividing cancer cells are most affected. MTX is used for ALL, lymphomas, osteosarcoma, choriocarcinoma, psoriasis, and rheumatoid arthritis. Leucovorin (folinic acid, N5-formyl-THF) rescue bypasses DHFR and restores normal cell folate after high-dose MTX.

questions.text: What are inhibitors of folic acid?
questions.answer: Sulfonamides, trimethoprim, and methotrexate.
questions.explanation: Folate pathway inhibitors act at different steps: (1) Sulfonamides — inhibit dihydropteroate synthase (bacterial only), blocking folate synthesis from PABA; (2) Trimethoprim — inhibits bacterial DHFR (selectively), blocking folate activation; (3) Methotrexate — inhibits mammalian (and bacterial) DHFR, blocking folate activation; used as anticancer and immunosuppressive agent. All three ultimately deprive cells of active THF, impairing DNA synthesis. Their clinical selectivity depends on their relative affinity for bacterial vs. mammalian enzymes.

questions.text: What are the sources of Vitamin B₁₂?
questions.answer: Meat, eggs, milk, and milk products. Vitamin B₁₂ is not present in plant sources.
questions.explanation: Vitamin B₁₂ (cobalamin) is synthesized exclusively by certain microorganisms (bacteria and archaea) and accumulates in animal tissues. There are NO plant sources of B₁₂ — making strict vegans entirely dependent on supplements or fortified foods. Richest dietary sources: liver (extremely high), other organ meats, clams, oysters, sardines, beef, dairy products, and eggs. B₁₂ in food is protein-bound and released by pepsin and gastric acid, then absorbed with the help of intrinsic factor (IF).

questions.text: What are the causes of Vitamin B₁₂ deficiency?
questions.answer: Nutritional deficiency, drug-induced deficiency (neomycin, alcohol), decreased absorption, pernicious anemia, atrophy of gastric mucosa, and pregnancy.
questions.explanation: B₁₂ deficiency causes: (1) Nutritional — strict veganism (no animal products); (2) Malabsorption — pernicious anemia (autoimmune lack of IF), gastrectomy, atrophic gastritis (H. pylori), ileal resection/Crohn's (terminal ileum is the absorption site), fish tapeworm (Diphyllobothrium latum competes for B₁₂); (3) Drug-induced — metformin (blocks B₁₂ absorption from ileal IF-B₁₂ receptor), neomycin, proton pump inhibitors (reduce gastric acid needed to free food-bound B₁₂), nitrous oxide (irreversibly oxidizes cobalt in B₁₂, inactivating methionine synthase); (4) Increased demand — pregnancy.

questions.text: Name a water-soluble vitamin that is stored in the body.
questions.answer: Vitamin B₁₂.
questions.explanation: Unlike other water-soluble vitamins that are rapidly excreted in urine, B₁₂ is stored in substantial amounts in the liver (3–5 mg total body stores, predominantly as adenosylcobalamin). This storage capacity explains why nutritional B₁₂ deficiency takes 3–5 years to develop even after complete dietary elimination (e.g., strict veganism).
