Clinical deficiency from malabsorption develops faster (1–2 years) because the enterohepatic circulation of B₁₂ is also disrupted.

questions.text: What is the metal present in Vitamin B₁₂?
questions.answer: Cobalt.
questions.explanation: Vitamin B₁₂ (cobalamin) is the only vitamin that contains a metal ion — cobalt (Co) — as an integral part of its structure. The cobalt atom is centrally positioned within the corrin ring and forms coordinate bonds with four nitrogen atoms of the ring and one nitrogen from the lower axial ligand (5,6-dimethylbenzimidazole). The upper axial ligand varies, defining the cobalamin form: cyanocobalamin (CN⁻, synthetic), hydroxocobalamin (OH⁻), methylcobalamin (CH₃⁻), or adenosylcobalamin (5'-deoxyadenosyl).

questions.text: Why is Vitamin B₁₂ red in color?
questions.answer: Because it contains the cobalt element, which imparts the red color.
questions.explanation: The red/pink color of vitamin B₁₂ (cyanocobalamin) is due to the cobalt ion within the corrin ring system, which has characteristic light absorption properties in the visible spectrum (absorption maxima around 361 nm and 550 nm). Different cobalamin forms show slightly different colors: cyanocobalamin is bright red; hydroxocobalamin is orange-red; methylcobalamin is yellow; adenosylcobalamin is deep red/orange. This distinctive color aids in identification and purification of B₁₂ preparations.

questions.text: What is the ring system present in Vitamin B₁₂?
questions.answer: Corrin ring.
questions.explanation: The corrin ring is the structural core of all cobalamins — a macrocyclic ring system similar to porphyrin (found in heme) but smaller and with one less methine bridge (A and D rings are directly connected, skipping one carbon). The corrin ring consists of four reduced pyrrole rings (A, B, C, D) with the cobalt atom coordinated at the center. Unlike porphyrins, the corrin ring is not fully conjugated. The 5,6-dimethylbenzimidazole nucleotide forms the lower axial ligand to cobalt.

questions.text: What is the transport form of Vitamin B₁₂?
questions.answer: Methyl-B₁₂ (methylcobalamin).
questions.explanation: Methylcobalamin is the predominant form of B₁₂ in blood plasma and the cytosolic form in cells. It serves as a coenzyme for methionine synthase, transferring its methyl group to homocysteine to form methionine and regenerating THF (releasing B₁₂ from the methyl folate trap). Adenosylcobalamin is the mitochondrial form, serving as a coenzyme for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase. After intestinal absorption (as hydroxocobalamin or cyanocobalamin), B₁₂ is converted to these active forms in tissues.

questions.text: What is the carrier of Vitamin B₁₂ in blood?
questions.answer: Transcobalamin-II — a glycoprotein that is the specific plasma carrier of newly absorbed B₁₂.
questions.explanation: B₁₂ transport proteins: (1) Transcobalamin-II (TC-II) — the functional transport protein carrying newly absorbed B₁₂ from intestine to tissues; TC-II–B₁₂ complex is taken up by cells via TC-II receptor (TCblR/CD320) by endocytosis; TC-II deficiency causes severe megaloblastic anemia despite normal serum B₁₂; (2) Transcobalamin-I (TC-I, haptocorrin R-binder) — produced by granulocytes; carries most circulating B₁₂ (~80%) but is metabolically inactive; elevated in myeloproliferative disorders; (3) Transcobalamin-III — similar to TC-I.

questions.text: What is the storage form of Vitamin B₁₂?
questions.answer: Stored in the liver in combination with transcobalamin-I (TC-I) or transcorrin.
questions.explanation: The liver is the principal B₁₂ storage organ, containing approximately 1–5 mg (representing years of reserve). Hepatic B₁₂ is stored bound to transcobalamin-I (haptocorrin/R-binder) predominantly as adenosylcobalamin. B₁₂ undergoes enterohepatic circulation: it is secreted in bile (bound to haptocorrin), released in the duodenum, rebound to IF, and reabsorbed in the ileum. Disruption of this recycling (e.g., by ileal disease) accelerates depletion of B₁₂ stores.

questions.text: What enzymes use Vitamin B₁₂ as a coenzyme?
questions.answer: Methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (isomerase).
questions.explanation: The two B₁₂-dependent enzymes in humans: (1) Methionine synthase (cytoplasmic) — uses methylcobalamin; transfers methyl group from N5-methyl-THF to homocysteine → methionine + THF; links folate and methionine cycles; (2) Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (mitochondrial) — uses adenosylcobalamin; converts L-methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA (TCA cycle entry); essential for catabolism of odd-chain fatty acids, branched-chain amino acids (Val, Ile), and threonine. Both reactions explain the biochemical abnormalities in B₁₂ deficiency: elevated homocysteine and methylmalonic acid.

questions.text: What abnormalities are seen in Vitamin B₁₂ deficiency?
questions.answer: Megaloblastic anemia, neurological manifestations, methylmalonic aciduria, and homocysteinuria.
questions.explanation: B₁₂ deficiency produces a dual pathology: (1) Hematological — megaloblastic (macrocytic hyperchromic) anemia due to impaired DNA synthesis from the methyl folate trap (functional THF deficiency); (2) Neurological — subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord (demyelination of posterior and lateral columns) → peripheral neuropathy, proprioception loss, spastic weakness; (3) Biochemical — elevated plasma/urine homocysteine (methionine synthase deficiency) and methylmalonic acid (methylmalonyl-CoA mutase deficiency). Elevated MMA is specific for B₁₂ deficiency (not folate deficiency).

questions.text: In Vitamin B₁₂ deficiency, what abnormalities are seen in urine?
questions.answer: Urine may contain methylmalonic acid, homocysteine, cystathionine, and formiminoglutamic acid (FIGLU).
questions.explanation: Urinary abnormalities in B₁₂ deficiency reflect impaired enzyme activities: (1) Methylmalonic aciduria — methylmalonyl-CoA mutase impairment (specific for B₁₂ deficiency; used diagnostically); (2) Homocysteinuria — methionine synthase impairment (also seen in folate and B₆ deficiency); (3) Cystathionuria — secondary to reduced methionine availability, impairing downstream transsulfuration; (4) FIGLU-uria — due to the methyl folate trap reducing available THF for FIGLU → glutamate conversion (also seen in folate deficiency). Elevated MMA distinguishes B₁₂ deficiency from isolated folate deficiency.

questions.text: What is megaloblastic anemia characterized by?
questions.answer: Macrocytic hyperchromic anemia due to abnormal DNA replication in hematopoietic tissue. It results from direct folate insufficiency or indirect cobalamin (B₁₂) insufficiency.
questions.explanation: Megaloblastic anemia features: (1) Peripheral blood: macrocytic red cells (MCV >100 fL), macro-ovalocytes, hypersegmented neutrophils (>5% with ≥5 lobes or any with ≥6 lobes — pathognomonic); (2) Bone marrow: megaloblasts (giant erythroid precursors with immature nucleus and mature cytoplasm — nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony), giant metamyelocytes; (3) Pancytopenia in severe cases (anemia + leukopenia + thrombocytopenia); (4) Elevated LDH and indirect bilirubin (ineffective erythropoiesis with intramedullary hemolysis).

questions.text: What neurological manifestations are seen in Vitamin B₁₂ deficiency?
questions.answer: Breakdown of myelin sheaths causing peripheral neuritis (numbness, tingling, weakness of extremities) and subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord (affecting both motor and sensory tracts).
questions.explanation: Subacute combined degeneration (SCD) of the spinal cord in B₁₂ deficiency: affects dorsal columns (vibration and proprioception loss → positive Romberg sign) and lateral corticospinal tracts (upper motor neuron signs → spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign). Peripheral neuropathy also occurs (glove-and-stocking sensory loss). The neurological damage is caused by deficient SAM-dependent methylation of myelin proteins and phospholipids (due to methionine deficiency). Crucially, neurological damage is NOT corrected by giving folic acid alone — which can actually mask and worsen the neuropathy.

questions.text: Explain why giving folic acid does not treat the macrocytic anemia of Vitamin B₁₂ deficiency.
questions.answer: Folic acid corrects the anemia but worsens neurological manifestations, as the underlying B₁₂ deficiency and resultant myelin damage remain untreated.
questions.explanation: This is the critical clinical pitfall: in B₁₂ deficiency, giving folic acid replenishes the one-carbon pool for DNA synthesis (correcting the hematological picture) but: (1) Does NOT restore methionine synthase activity (still blocked by B₁₂ deficiency); (2) Does NOT restore methylmalonyl-CoA mutase activity; (3) Does NOT correct the SAM deficiency causing demyelination; (4) May actually accelerate neurological deterioration by increasing metabolic demand on remaining B₁₂-dependent pathways. Therefore, the cause of macrocytic anemia (B₁₂ vs. folate) MUST be established before treatment.

questions.text: What abnormal compounds are excreted in Vitamin B₁₂ deficiency?
questions.answer: Increased urinary methylmalonyl-CoA (methylmalonic aciduria) and increased urinary homocysteine (homocysteinuria).
questions.explanation: The two key metabolic markers of B₁₂ deficiency: (1) Methylmalonic acid (MMA) — elevated due to methylmalonyl-CoA mutase impairment; highly specific for B₁₂ deficiency (not elevated in isolated folate deficiency); urinary MMA >3.6 μmol/mmol creatinine is diagnostic; serum MMA >0.4 μmol/L is abnormal; (2) Homocysteine — elevated due to methionine synthase impairment; also elevated in folate and B₆ deficiency (less specific). Combined elevation of both MMA and homocysteine is diagnostic of functional B₁₂ deficiency.

questions.text: What is the folate trap?
questions.answer: The production of N5-methyl-THF (methyl-THFA) is an irreversible step. The only way to regenerate free THF from it is via methionine synthase (a B₁₂-dependent enzyme). When B₁₂ is deficient, this reaction is blocked, and folate becomes trapped as N5-methyl-THF — this is the methyl folate trap.
questions.explanation: The methyl folate trap mechanism: N5,N10-methylene-THF is reduced to N5-methyl-THF by methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR) — an irreversible reaction. N5-methyl-THF can only donate its methyl group via methionine synthase (which requires B₁₂ as methylcobalamin). In B₁₂ deficiency, methionine synthase is inactive, N5-methyl-THF accumulates (cannot be recycled to THF), and all other THF forms (needed for purine and dTMP synthesis) are depleted. This explains why B₁₂ deficiency produces megaloblastic anemia identical to folate deficiency.

questions.text: What is the clinical importance of the folate trap?
questions.answer: It leads to functional folic acid scarcity (folate deficiency) in the context of B₁₂ deficiency, explaining the megaloblastic anemia seen in B₁₂ deficiency.
questions.explanation: The methyl folate trap has major clinical implications: (1) B₁₂ deficiency produces megaloblastic anemia that appears identical to folate deficiency on blood film (both cause macrocytic hyperchromic anemia); (2) Serum folate may appear normal or even elevated in B₁₂ deficiency (trapped N5-methyl-THF remains in circulation but is metabolically unavailable); (3) Red cell folate is low in both conditions; (4) Treatment with folic acid corrects the anemia in B₁₂ deficiency (temporarily replenishing THF via alternative pathways) but masks the B₁₂ deficiency while neurological damage progresses.

questions.text: What is the explanation for demyelination in Vitamin B₁₂ deficiency?
questions.answer: B₁₂ deficiency → reduced methionine → insufficient SAM → deficient methylation of phosphatidylethanolamine to phosphatidylcholine → deficient myelin sheath formation.
questions.explanation: The demyelination mechanism: Methionine synthase (B₁₂-dependent) converts homocysteine → methionine → S-adenosylmethionine (SAM). SAM is the methyl donor for phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) → phosphatidylcholine (PC) methylation via PE-methyltransferase. PC is an essential component of myelin sheaths. In B₁₂ deficiency: SAM ↓ → PE methylation ↓ → PC ↓ → myelin synthesis impaired → myelin breakdown. Additionally, methylmalonyl-CoA accumulation (from deficient mutase) may lead to incorporation of abnormal odd-chain fatty acids into myelin, further disrupting its structure.

questions.text: What is the cause of pernicious anemia?
questions.answer: An autoimmune disease with familial background. Antibodies are generated against intrinsic factor (IF), leading to its deficiency and defective absorption of B₁₂.
questions.explanation: Pernicious anemia is the most common cause of B₁₂ deficiency in developed countries. Autoimmune features: (1) Type I antibodies (blocking antibodies, ~70% of patients) — prevent B₁₂ from binding to IF; (2) Type II antibodies (binding antibodies, ~40%) — bind the IF–B₁₂ complex, preventing ileal absorption; (3) Anti-parietal cell antibodies (~90%) — destroy gastric parietal cells, reducing both IF and HCl secretion. Associated with other autoimmune conditions (thyroid disease, Type 1 diabetes, Addison's disease). Treatment: regular IM hydroxocobalamin injections (bypassing the IF-dependent absorption route).

questions.text: What is the difference between folate deficiency and Vitamin B₁₂ deficiency?
questions.answer: Folate deficiency: macrocytic anemia only. B₁₂ deficiency: macrocytic anemia AND neurological symptoms (subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord).
questions.explanation: Key differentiating features: Folate deficiency — macrocytic anemia; elevated homocysteine; normal MMA; normal neurological exam; responds to folate treatment; common causes: poor diet, pregnancy, malabsorption, drugs. B₁₂ deficiency — macrocytic anemia + neurological manifestations (SCD, peripheral neuropathy); elevated both homocysteine AND MMA; requires B₁₂ (not folate) treatment; common causes: pernicious anemia, veganism, ileal disease. Critical rule: ALWAYS rule out B₁₂ deficiency before treating macrocytic anemia with folate, to avoid neurological deterioration.

questions.text: Enumerate vitamins important for transmethylation.
questions.answer: Folic acid (in its active THF form) and Vitamin B₁₂ (cobamides).
questions.explanation: Transmethylation reactions — transfer of methyl (–CH₃) groups — require: (1) SAM (S-adenosylmethionine) as the universal methyl donor (methylates DNA, RNA, proteins, phospholipids, catecholamines); (2) Methionine regeneration from homocysteine requires B₁₂ (methionine synthase uses N5-methyl-THF as methyl donor) and folate (provides N5-methyl-THF); (3) Additionally, betaine (from choline oxidation) can remethylate homocysteine via betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase (B₁₂-independent). Thus, folate and B₁₂ are both essential for maintaining the transmethylation cycle.

questions.text: What is the daily requirement of Vitamin B₁₂?
questions.answer: 1–2 μg/day.
questions.explanation: The RDA for B₁₂ in adults is 2.4 μg/day. Requirements are higher during pregnancy (2.6 μg/day) and lactation (2.8 μg/day). Despite the small daily requirement, the body maintains large hepatic reserves (3–5 mg), sufficient for 3–5 years. Since B₁₂ is absent from plant foods, strict vegans need supplementation with cyanocobalamin (the stable synthetic form) or consumption of B₁₂-fortified foods (plant milks, nutritional yeast, fortified cereals).

questions.text: A patient who has undergone gastrectomy is likely to develop deficiency of which vitamin?
questions.answer: Vitamin B₁₂.
questions.explanation: Gastrectomy (total or partial) causes B₁₂ deficiency by: (1) Removing parietal cells that produce intrinsic factor (IF) — essential for ileal B₁₂ absorption; (2) Reducing gastric acid secretion needed to release protein-bound B₁₂ from food. Since the liver stores 3–5 mg of B₁₂, deficiency typically manifests 3–5 years post-gastrectomy. Post-gastrectomy patients require lifelong B₁₂ supplementation, usually by intramuscular injection (bypassing the absent IF-dependent mechanism) or high-dose oral B₁₂ (passive absorption).

questions.text: Which vitamin is totally absent in plant sources?
questions.answer: Vitamin B₁₂.
questions.explanation: Vitamin B₁₂ is exclusively synthesized by microorganisms (bacteria and archaea) and is not produced by any plant, fungus, or animal. Animals (including humans) obtain B₁₂ by consuming animal products (meat, dairy, eggs) where B₁₂ from gut microbes or dietary sources has bioaccumulated. Some fermented plant foods (tempeh, certain algae like nori) may contain B₁₂ analogues, but these are largely inactive in humans or present in negligible quantities. This makes B₁₂ supplementation critical for strict vegans.

questions.text: Vitamin B₁₂ is absorbed from where?
questions.answer: The terminal ileum.
questions.explanation: B₁₂ absorption pathway: (1) Food-bound B₁₂ is released by gastric acid and pepsin; (2) Free B₁₂ binds to haptocorrin (R-binder) in the stomach; (3) In the duodenum, pancreatic proteases degrade haptocorrin, releasing B₁₂; (4) Free B₁₂ binds intrinsic factor (IF, secreted by gastric parietal cells), forming the IF–B₁₂ complex; (5) The IF–B₁₂ complex travels to the terminal ileum, where it binds the cubilin receptor (CUBN) and is absorbed by endocytosis; (6) Inside ileal cells, IF is degraded and B₁₂ is transferred to transcobalamin-II for portal transport.

questions.text: Enumerate vitamins synthesized by intestinal bacteria.
questions.answer: Vitamin K, biotin, and Vitamin B₁₂.
questions.explanation: Gut microbiota (primarily in the large intestine/colon) synthesize: (1) Vitamin K₂ (menaquinones) — major source in some populations; primarily synthesized by Bacteroides, E. coli, and other anaerobes; (2) Biotin — synthesized by Bacteroides, Fusobacterium, and other colonic bacteria; contributes to biotin status; (3) Vitamin B₁₂ — synthesized by Pseudomonas, Propionibacterium, and others, but mainly in the colon, where absorption is minimal (B₁₂ absorption requires IF and terminal ileum). This explains why colonic B₁₂ does not prevent deficiency, unlike K and biotin which can be partially absorbed.

questions.text: 151. Can the body utilize B₁₂ synthesized in large intestine?
questions.answer: No, because B₁₂ is not absorbed through the mucosa of large intestine.
questions.explanation: Vitamin B₁₂ absorption requires intrinsic factor (IF) secreted by gastric parietal cells, and absorption occurs only at the terminal ileum. The large intestine lacks the specific receptors and transport mechanisms for B₁₂ absorption; therefore, B₁₂ synthesized by colonic bacteria cannot be utilized and is excreted in feces.

questions.text: 152. Enumerate coenzymes derived from vitamins.
questions.answer: TPP, FMN, FAD, NAD, NADP, PLP, CoASH, Lipoic acid, Cobalamin, and Vitamin C.
questions.explanation: Each coenzyme is derived from a specific vitamin: TPP from Thiamine (B₁); FMN and FAD from Riboflavin (B₂); NAD and NADP from Niacin (B₃); CoASH from Pantothenic acid (B₅); PLP from Pyridoxine (B₆); Cobalamin from B₁₂; Lipoic acid is a vitamin-like cofactor; and Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) acts directly as an electron-donating coenzyme in hydroxylation reactions.

questions.text: 153. What is the chemical structure of Vitamin C?
questions.answer: L-ascorbic acid.
questions.explanation: Vitamin C is L-ascorbic acid, a six-carbon water-soluble lactone structurally related to glucose. It contains an enediol group on carbons 2 and 3 responsible for its potent reducing and antioxidant properties. It is reversibly oxidized to L-dehydroascorbic acid, which retains biological activity.

questions.text: 154. How is Vitamin C synthesized?
questions.answer: Man and primates cannot synthesize ascorbic acid. Lower animals can synthesize it from glucose through the glucuronic acid pathway.
questions.explanation: In most mammals, glucose is converted via UDP-glucuronate → glucuronate → L-gulonate → L-gulonolactone, then oxidized to L-ascorbic acid by the enzyme L-gulonolactone oxidase. Humans, primates, and guinea pigs lack a functional gene for this enzyme due to mutation, making Vitamin C an essential dietary nutrient for these species.

questions.text: 155. What are the major functions of ascorbic acid?
questions.answer: Ascorbic acid promotes collagen formation through its action on post-translational hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues into hydroxyproline and hydroxylysine residues.
questions.explanation: Ascorbic acid is an essential cofactor for prolyl hydroxylase and lysyl hydroxylase enzymes. These enzymes catalyze the post-translational hydroxylation of proline and lysine in procollagen chains, which is critical for stable triple-helix formation and collagen cross-linking. Deficiency impairs collagen synthesis, causing the vascular and connective tissue fragility seen in scurvy.

questions.text: 156. What are the other functions of ascorbic acid?
questions.answer: Iron absorption from the intestine, reconversion of methemoglobin to hemoglobin, carnitine synthesis, catecholamine synthesis, steroid hormone synthesis, oxidation of parahydroxyphenyl pyruvate to homogentisic acid. Ascorbic acid acts as a specific reducing agent giving electrons to ferric ions, cupric ions, and metal ions bound to various cytochromes and oxygen.
questions.explanation: Ascorbic acid reduces dietary non-heme Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺ enhancing intestinal absorption. It is a cofactor for dopamine β-hydroxylase (catecholamine synthesis), for two hydroxylation steps in carnitine biosynthesis, for steroidogenic hydroxylases in the adrenal cortex, and for 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase in tyrosine catabolism. Its broad electron-donating ability to metal ion centers underpins its role as a universal reducing agent and antioxidant.

questions.text: 157. Which vitamin is required for post-translational modifications?
questions.answer: Ascorbic acid.
questions.explanation: Ascorbic acid (Vitamin C) is required as a cofactor for prolyl-4-hydroxylase and lysyl hydroxylase, which carry out post-translational hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues in procollagen. These modifications are essential for the stability of the collagen triple helix and subsequent extracellular cross-linking. Without Vitamin C, these Fe²⁺-dependent dioxygenases are inactivated.

questions.text: 158. What are the vitamins that act as antioxidants?
questions.answer: Vitamins E, A, and C.
questions.explanation: Vitamin E (α-tocopherol) is the primary lipid-soluble antioxidant protecting cell membranes from lipid peroxidation by scavenging peroxyl radicals. β-Carotene (pro-vitamin A) quenches singlet oxygen and reactive species. Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is the major water-soluble antioxidant and regenerates active Vitamin E from its radical form, forming a cooperative antioxidant network.

questions.text: 159. What is the daily requirement of ascorbic acid?
questions.answer: 75 mg/day.
questions.explanation: The recommended daily allowance (RDA) for Vitamin C is approximately 75 mg/day. Requirements increase during pregnancy, lactation, infection, surgery, and in smokers due to increased oxidative stress and accelerated utilization.

questions.text: 160. Scurvy is due to the deficiency of which vitamin?
questions.answer: Ascorbic acid.
questions.explanation: Scurvy develops when body stores of Vitamin C fall below critical levels. The hallmark pathology is defective collagen synthesis: without adequate hydroxylation of proline and lysine, the procollagen triple helix is unstable and cannot be properly cross-linked, leading to fragile blood vessels, connective tissue breakdown, bleeding, and the classic clinical features of scurvy.

questions.text: 161. How long can Vitamin C be stored in the body?
questions.answer: 3 months.
questions.explanation: The human body stores approximately 1,500 mg of Vitamin C, primarily in the adrenal glands, pituitary, and leukocytes. On a Vitamin C-free diet, these stores are depleted over approximately 3 months before clinical signs of scurvy appear. This explains the historical occurrence of scurvy in sailors after prolonged voyages without fresh fruits and vegetables.

questions.text: 162. What are the deficiency manifestations of Scurvy?
questions.answer: Bleeding into gum, muscles, joints, kidneys, gastrointestinal tract and pericardium (due to decreased collagen formation); behavioral change due to decrease in neurotransmitters; severe emotional disturbances; general weakness (due to decrease in carnitine and fatty acids oxidation).
questions.explanation: The multisystem manifestations reflect the wide-ranging roles of Vitamin C: (1) Vascular fragility due to defective collagen in vessel walls causes perifollicular hemorrhages, gingival bleeding, hemarthrosis, and pericardial effusion. (2) Neuropsychiatric symptoms result from impaired dopamine β-hydroxylase activity, reducing norepinephrine synthesis. (3) Fatigue and weakness result from impaired carnitine biosynthesis, reducing mitochondrial fatty acid β-oxidation and energy production.

questions.text: 163. What are the important features of scurvy?
questions.answer: Hemorrhagic tendency, microcytic anemia, bone pain, bleeding gums.
questions.explanation: Key features of scurvy: (1) Hemorrhagic tendency — perifollicular hemorrhages, ecchymoses, and internal bleeding due to fragile collagen-deficient vessel walls. (2) Microcytic anemia — due to chronic blood loss and impaired iron absorption. (3) Bone pain — defective osteoid matrix formation in growing bones. (4) Bleeding spongy gums — classic feature due to periodontal collagen breakdown and capillary fragility.

questions.text: 164. What are vitamins alcoholic in nature?
questions.answer: Vitamins A, D, E, C, B₁, B₂, B₆, pantothenic acid, and folic acid.
questions.explanation: These vitamins contain one or more hydroxyl (-OH) groups in their chemical structure, classifying them as alcohols or polyols. Examples: Vitamin A (retinol — primary alcohol), Vitamin D (cholecalciferol — secondary alcohol), Vitamin E (tocopherol — phenolic alcohol), Vitamin C (ascorbic acid — enediol lactone), Vitamin B₁ (hydroxyethyl thiazole group), Vitamin B₂ (ribitol side chain), Vitamin B₆ (pyridoxol), Pantothenic acid, and Folic acid (hydroxyl-bearing pteridine ring).

questions.text: 165. What are sulfur-containing vitamins?
questions.answer: B₁ (thiamine), Biotin, and Lipoic acid.
questions.explanation: Sulfur-containing vitamins: (1) Thiamine (B₁) contains a thiazole ring with a sulfur atom, essential for TPP coenzyme function in oxidative decarboxylation. (2) Biotin contains a tetrahydrothiophene ring with sulfur, functioning as a CO₂ carrier in carboxylation reactions. (3) Lipoic acid contains a dithiolane ring with two sulfur atoms, acting as a redox-active swinging arm in α-keto acid dehydrogenase complexes.

questions.text: 166. What are sulfur-containing coenzymes?
questions.answer: TPP, Biotin, CoASH, Lipoic acid, and Glutathione (GSH).
questions.explanation: Sulfur-containing coenzymes: (1) TPP — thiazole ring sulfur participates in active aldehyde transfer. (2) Biotin — tetrahydrothiophene ring sulfur essential for CO₂ carboxylation. (3) CoASH — contains a thiol (-SH) group from cysteamine; forms high-energy thioester bonds with acyl groups. (4) Lipoic acid — dithiolane ring undergoes redox cycling, transferring acyl groups and electrons. (5) Glutathione (GSH) — tripeptide (Glu-Cys-Gly) with a cysteine thiol; major intracellular antioxidant and substrate for glutathione peroxidase.

questions.text: 167. What are the vitamins important for erythropoiesis?
questions.answer: Folic acid and B₁₂.
questions.explanation: Folic acid (as tetrahydrofolate) and Vitamin B₁₂ are essential for purine and thymidylate synthesis required for DNA replication in rapidly dividing erythroblasts. B₁₂ is also needed to regenerate active THF from methyl-THF (methyl-trap hypothesis). Deficiency of either vitamin impairs nuclear maturation of red cell precursors while cytoplasmic hemoglobin development continues, producing megaloblasts and macrocytic megaloblastic anemia.

questions.text: 168. What is the importance of choline?
questions.answer: (1) It enters in the formation of lecithin, plasmalogen, and sphingomyelin. (2) It has a lipotropic action i.e. it prevents fatty liver. (3) It enters in the formation of acetylcholine. (4) Oxidation of choline gives betaine. Betaine functions as a methyl donor in transmethylation reactions.
questions.explanation: Choline's biochemical roles: (1) Structural — as the head group of phosphatidylcholine (lecithin), plasmalogen, and sphingomyelin, essential for membrane integrity and VLDL assembly. (2) Lipotropic — promotes hepatic VLDL export of fat, preventing hepatic steatosis. (3) Neurotransmission — acetylated by choline acetyltransferase to form acetylcholine, the neurotransmitter at neuromuscular junctions and parasympathetic synapses. (4) One-carbon metabolism — choline is oxidized to betaine, which donates a methyl group to homocysteine forming methionine via betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase.

questions.text: 169. Explain why choline is not considered a vitamin?
questions.answer: Because it is needed in a relatively big amount, it can be formed in the body from serine, and it enters in the structure of tissues.
questions.explanation: A vitamin by definition is an organic micronutrient required in trace amounts that cannot be synthesized adequately by the body. Choline fails this definition because: (1) it is required in gram quantities (~400–550 mg/day), far exceeding typical vitamin requirements; (2) it can be endogenously synthesized in the liver via three sequential SAM-dependent methylations of phosphatidylethanolamine (derived from serine); and (3) it is a structural component of cell membranes and lipoproteins. Therefore, choline is classified as an essential nutrient but not a classic vitamin.

questions.text: 170. What is the importance of inositol?
questions.answer: It enters in the structure of phosphatidylinositol → Inositol triphosphate (IP₃) → Second messenger for hormonal action.
questions.explanation: Phosphatidylinositol (PI) in the inner plasma membrane leaflet is phosphorylated to PIP₂. Upon activation of Gq-coupled receptors, phospholipase C-β cleaves PIP₂ into: (1) IP₃ — releases Ca²⁺ from the endoplasmic reticulum, activating calmodulin-dependent kinases; and (2) Diacylglycerol (DAG) — activates protein kinase C (PKC). This IP₃/DAG pathway is a major second messenger cascade linking extracellular hormonal signals to intracellular cellular responses.

questions.text: 171. What is the importance of lipoic acid?
questions.answer: It acts as a coenzyme in the decarboxylation of α-keto acids, e.g., pyruvate and α-ketoglutarate.
questions.explanation: Lipoic acid is covalently attached to the E2 (dihydrolipoamide acyltransferase) subunit of α-keto acid dehydrogenase complexes. Its dithiolane ring acts as a flexible swinging arm that: (1) accepts the acyl group from the hydroxyethyl-TPP intermediate on E1 following oxidative decarboxylation; (2) transfers the acyl group to CoASH generating acetyl-CoA or succinyl-CoA; and (3) is reoxidized by E3 (FAD-dependent dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase), which transfers electrons to NAD⁺. It thus functions in both the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex and the α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex.

questions.text: 1. Pyridoxal phosphate is a cofactor for which of the following enzymatic reaction?
optionReasons: Wrong: CO₂ fixation is the role of Biotin (e.g., in pyruvate carboxylase), not PLP.
Wrong: Oxidation-reduction reactions are carried out by FAD and NAD⁺ coenzymes derived from riboflavin and niacin, not PLP.

Correct: Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) is the essential coenzyme for all transaminase (aminotransferase) reactions, forming a Schiff base with the amino group of the substrate to transfer it to an α-keto acid.
Wrong: One-carbon group transfer is the function of Tetrahydrofolate (THF), not PLP.
Wrong: Decarboxylation of α-keto acids (e.g., pyruvate) requires Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) and Lipoic acid within the dehydrogenase complex, not PLP.
questions.explanation: PLP (pyridoxal phosphate), derived from vitamin B₆, functions as a coenzyme in transamination reactions (e.g., AST and ALT), amino acid decarboxylations (e.g., DOPA decarboxylase), and other reactions involving amino acid metabolism. In transamination, PLP forms an aldimine (Schiff base) with the α-amino group of the donor amino acid, transfers the amino group to itself becoming pyridoxamine phosphate (PMP), then donates it to an α-keto acid to form a new amino acid.

questions.text: 2. Which one of the following statements concerning vitamin E is INCORRECT?
options: A. Diet rich in vitamin E decreases the risk of heart diseases.
B. It inactivates toxic oxygen superoxide and free radicals.
C. It removes peroxide formation in polyunsaturated fatty acids.
D. Its deficiency usually occurs in premature infants.
E. Long term deficiency leads to night blindness.
optionReasons: Wrong (i.e., this statement IS correct): Vitamin E's antioxidant action reduces LDL oxidation and lipid peroxidation, which are linked to atherosclerosis and heart disease risk.
Wrong (i.e., this statement IS correct): Vitamin E (α-tocopherol) neutralizes superoxide radicals and other reactive oxygen species by donating a hydrogen atom, quenching the radical chain reaction.
Wrong (i.e., this statement IS correct): Vitamin E interrupts lipid peroxidation chain reactions in polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA)-rich cell membranes by scavenging peroxyl radicals.

Wrong (i.e., this statement IS correct): Premature infants have low adipose tissue stores and immature antioxidant defenses, making them particularly susceptible to Vitamin E deficiency and hemolytic anemia.

Correct (i.e., this statement IS INCORRECT): Night blindness is due to deficiency of Vitamin A (retinol), not Vitamin E. Long-term Vitamin E deficiency causes hemolytic anemia, peripheral neuropathy, and spinocerebellar ataxia.
questions.explanation: Night blindness (nyctalopia) is specifically caused by Vitamin A deficiency, because retinal (derived from retinol) is the chromophore of rhodopsin in rod photoreceptors. Vitamin E deficiency does not affect the visual cycle. Long-term Vitamin E deficiency causes neurological deficits (peripheral neuropathy, ataxia due to posterior column and spinocerebellar tract degeneration) and hemolytic anemia in premature infants.

questions.text: 3. Which one of the following statements concerning water soluble vitamins is INCORRECT?
options: A. Biotin functions as coenzyme for oxidative decarboxylation of α-keto acids.
B. Pantothenic acid is a part of acyl carrier protein (ACP).
C. Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) is essential for heme metabolism.
D. People who depend on corn in their diet may develop pellagra.
E. Folate deficiency may accompany vitamin B₁₂ deficiency due to complexity between the two vitamins.
optionReasons: Correct (i.e., this statement IS INCORRECT): Oxidative decarboxylation of α-keto acids (e.g., pyruvate → acetyl-CoA) requires TPP, Lipoic acid, CoASH, FAD, and NAD⁺ — NOT Biotin. Biotin is the coenzyme for carboxylation reactions (CO₂ fixation), such as pyruvate carboxylase and acetyl-CoA carboxylase.

Wrong (i.e., this statement IS correct): Pantothenic acid (B₅) is a structural component of both CoASH and the 4'-phosphopantetheine prosthetic group of acyl carrier protein (ACP) in fatty acid synthase.

Wrong (i.e., this statement IS correct): PLP is the coenzyme for δ-aminolevulinate (ALA) synthase, the first and rate-limiting enzyme of heme biosynthesis, catalyzing condensation of succinyl-CoA and glycine.

Wrong (i.e., this statement IS correct): Corn (maize) is rich in bound niacin (niacytin) that is not bioavailable, and poor in tryptophan (a niacin precursor). Populations relying heavily on corn without alkali treatment (nixtamalization) develop pellagra (niacin deficiency).

Wrong (i.e., this statement IS correct): The methyl-trap hypothesis explains how B₁₂ deficiency traps folate as methyl-THF, making it unavailable for DNA synthesis, thus causing folate-like deficiency even when dietary folate is adequate.
questions.explanation: Biotin is the coenzyme specifically for carboxylation reactions, acting as a CO₂ carrier. It is covalently bound to the enzyme and accepts CO₂ from bicarbonate (using ATP) to form carboxybiotin, which then transfers CO₂ to the substrate. Key biotin-dependent enzymes include pyruvate carboxylase, acetyl-CoA carboxylase, propionyl-CoA carboxylase, and methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase. Oxidative decarboxylation of α-keto acids is an entirely different reaction requiring a completely different set of cofactors (TPP, lipoic acid, CoASH, FAD, NAD⁺).

questions.text: 4. Vitamin K:
options: A. Is a water soluble vitamin.
D. Present normally in the intestine of newborn infants.
E. Long use of dicumarol promotes its action.
optionReasons: Wrong: Vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin (along with Vitamins A, D, and E); it requires dietary fat and bile acids for intestinal absorption.
Wrong: Vitamin K₂ (menaquinone) is the naturally occurring form synthesized by intestinal bacteria. Vitamin K₃ (menadione) is the synthetic form.

Correct: Vitamin K is essential for the γ-carboxylation of glutamate residues in coagulation factors II (prothrombin), VII, IX, and X, as well as anticoagulant proteins C and S. This carboxylation is necessary for their Ca²⁺-binding ability and clot formation.

Wrong: Newborn infants have a sterile intestine at birth and lack colonic bacteria that synthesize Vitamin K₂. This is why neonates are routinely given prophylactic Vitamin K₁ at birth to prevent hemorrhagic disease of the newborn.

Wrong: Dicumarol (and warfarin) are Vitamin K antagonists — they inhibit vitamin K epoxide reductase, blocking the regeneration of active reduced Vitamin K, thereby OPPOSING (not promoting) its action.
questions.explanation: Vitamin K is indispensable for blood coagulation. It serves as a cofactor for γ-glutamyl carboxylase, which carboxylates specific glutamate residues in the vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X) and regulatory proteins (C, S, Z). The resulting γ-carboxyglutamate (Gla) residues chelate Ca²⁺, anchoring these proteins to phospholipid surfaces of activated platelets and endothelium — essential for the coagulation cascade. Vitamin K cycles between its reduced (KH₂) and oxidized (K epoxide) forms; dicumarol blocks this recycling.

questions.text: 5. Which one of the following statements concerning L-ascorbic acid is INCORRECT?
options: A. Dehydro-L-ascorbic acid is inactive form of vitamin C.
B. It is cofactor in hydroxylation of proline and lysine.
D. Long term deficiency leads to scurvy.
E. It acts as reducing agent and important for iron absorption.
optionReasons: Correct (i.e., this statement IS INCORRECT): Dehydro-L-ascorbic acid is actually the ACTIVE oxidized form of Vitamin C, not the inactive form. It retains biological activity and can be reduced back to L-ascorbic acid intracellularly.

Wrong (i.e., this statement IS correct): Ascorbic acid maintains the Fe²⁺ state of prolyl-4-hydroxylase and lysyl hydroxylase, making it an essential cofactor for post-translational hydroxylation of proline and lysine in procollagen.
Wrong (i.e., this statement IS correct): Ascorbic acid is a potent water-soluble antioxidant that scavenges reactive oxygen species and regenerates oxidized Vitamin E.

Wrong (i.e., this statement IS correct): Scurvy results from prolonged Vitamin C deficiency (typically after ~3 months of depletion), causing defective collagen synthesis and widespread hemorrhagic manifestations.

Wrong (i.e., this statement IS correct): Ascorbic acid reduces dietary non-heme iron from Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺ in the intestinal lumen, significantly enhancing its absorption through divalent metal transporter-1 (DMT-1).
questions.explanation: L-ascorbic acid (reduced form) and dehydro-L-ascorbic acid (oxidized form) both possess biological vitamin C activity. Dehydroascorbic acid is transported into cells via GLUT transporters and is rapidly reduced back to ascorbic acid intracellularly. Therefore, calling it 'inactive' is incorrect — it is a biologically active form that participates in the redox cycle of Vitamin C.

questions.text: 6. Which one of the following statements concerning niacin is CORRECT?
options: A. It is a coenzyme for carboxylation reactions.
B. Is the precursor of FAD coenzyme.
C. Its deficiency leads to Beri beri.
D. It is essential for formation of the coenzymes NAD and NADP⁺.
E. It is rich in maize.
optionReasons: Wrong: Carboxylation reactions use Biotin as a coenzyme, not niacin. Niacin functions in oxidation-reduction reactions.
Wrong: FAD (flavin adenine dinucleotide) is derived from Riboflavin (Vitamin B₂), not niacin.
Wrong: Beri beri is caused by Thiamine (Vitamin B₁) deficiency, not niacin deficiency. Niacin deficiency causes Pellagra.

Correct: Niacin (nicotinic acid or nicotinamide) is the precursor of NAD⁺ (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) and NADP⁺ (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate), which are essential coenzymes in over 200 oxidoreductase reactions in cellular metabolism.
Wrong: Maize (corn) is notably POOR in bioavailable niacin (niacin is bound as niacytin) and poor in tryptophan, which is why corn-dependent diets predispose to pellagra rather than preventing it.
questions.explanation: Niacin (B₃) is incorporated into NAD⁺ and NADP⁺, the universal electron-carrying coenzymes involved in catabolic oxidation reactions (NAD⁺, accepting electrons → NADH) and anabolic reductive biosynthesis (NADPH, donating electrons). Niacin can be synthesized endogenously from tryptophan (60 mg tryptophan → 1 mg niacin), which is why high-protein diets can partially meet niacin requirements. Niacin deficiency causes the 4 D's of pellagra: Dermatitis, Diarrhea, Dementia, and Death.

questions.text: 7. A deficiency of pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) may be accompanied by all the following EXCEPT:
options: A. Disturbance in amino acids metabolism.
optionReasons: Wrong (i.e., this IS a feature of PLP deficiency): PLP is a coenzyme for virtually all reactions of amino acid metabolism including transamination, decarboxylation, and desulfuration, so its deficiency severely disturbs amino acid metabolism.

Wrong (i.e., this IS a feature of PLP deficiency): PLP is essential for glutamate decarboxylase, which produces GABA (γ-aminobutyric acid), the main inhibitory neurotransmitter. PLP deficiency reduces GABA → neuronal hyperexcitability → convulsions, especially in infants.

Wrong (i.e., this IS a feature of PLP deficiency): PLP is required for the conversion of tryptophan to niacin (via kynureninase, a PLP-dependent enzyme). PLP deficiency impairs this pathway, reducing niacin synthesis and potentially causing pellagra-like symptoms.

Correct (i.e., this is EXCEPT — NOT caused by PLP deficiency): Scurvy is caused exclusively by Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) deficiency, which impairs collagen hydroxylation. PLP deficiency has no role in collagen synthesis.

Wrong (i.e., this IS a feature of PLP deficiency): PLP is the coenzyme for δ-ALA synthase, the rate-limiting enzyme of heme synthesis. PLP deficiency impairs heme production → sideroblastic (microcytic hypochromic) anemia with iron accumulation in erythroblast mitochondria.
questions.explanation: PLP (pyridoxal phosphate) is involved in amino acid metabolism, neurotransmitter synthesis (GABA, serotonin, dopamine, norepinephrine), heme synthesis (δ-ALA synthase), and tryptophan-to-niacin conversion. However, scurvy is entirely unrelated to B₆ — it results from ascorbic acid deficiency impairing prolyl and lysyl hydroxylation in collagen biosynthesis. PLP deficiency instead causes amino acid metabolic disorders, convulsions, secondary pellagra, and sideroblastic anemia.

questions.text: 8. Which one of the following statements concerning vitamin B₁₂ is INCORRECT?
options: A. It is red in color.
B. It is a cofactor for conversion of homocysteine into methionine.
C. It requires intrinsic factor for its absorption.
D. Strict vegetarians develop B₁₂ deficiency.
optionReasons: Wrong (i.e., this IS correct): Vitamin B₁₂ (cyanocobalamin) is indeed red in color due to the cobalt atom at the center of its corrin ring, which absorbs light in the red wavelength spectrum.
Wrong (i.e., this IS correct): Methylcobalamin (a form of B₁₂) is the coenzyme for methionine synthase, which methylates homocysteine to form methionine using methyl-THF as the methyl donor.

Wrong (i.e., this IS correct): B₁₂ binds to intrinsic factor (IF), a glycoprotein secreted by gastric parietal cells. The IF-B₁₂ complex is absorbed by specific receptors (cubilin) in the terminal ileum.

Wrong (i.e., this IS correct): B₁₂ is found exclusively in animal-derived foods. Strict (vegan) vegetarians who consume no animal products will develop B₁₂ deficiency over time, leading to megaloblastic anemia and neurological damage.

Correct (i.e., this IS INCORRECT): Vitamin B₁₂ contains a CORRIN ring (not a heme ring) with cobalt at its center. Heme contains a porphyrin ring with iron (Fe) at its center. These are structurally distinct macrocyclic systems.
questions.explanation: Vitamin B₁₂ (cobalamin) is unique in containing a corrin ring — a tetrapyrrole macrocycle similar to but distinct from porphyrin. The corrin ring coordinates a central cobalt atom, which is why it is called cobalamin. In contrast, heme is an iron-porphyrin complex. The cobalt in B₁₂ can exist in Co³⁺ (cyanocobalamin), Co²⁺, or Co¹⁺ forms; the Co¹⁺ form (cob(I)alamin) is the catalytically active nucleophile in cobalamin-dependent reactions.

questions.text: 9. Vitamin K plays a role in biosynthesis of:
optionReasons: Wrong: Collagen synthesis requires Vitamin C (for prolyl/lysyl hydroxylation). Vitamin K has no role in collagen or elastin biosynthesis.

Correct: Vitamin K is the cofactor for γ-glutamyl carboxylase, which carboxylates glutamate residues in prothrombin (Factor II) and osteocalcin (bone Gla protein), enabling their Ca²⁺-binding function.
Wrong: Heparin and heparan sulfate are glycosaminoglycans synthesized independently of Vitamin K via proteoglycan biosynthesis pathways.
Wrong: Prostaglandins and leukotrienes are eicosanoids derived from arachidonic acid via cyclooxygenase and lipoxygenase pathways, requiring no vitamin K.
Wrong: Electron transport in the mitochondrial respiratory chain involves FAD, NAD⁺, CoQ (ubiquinone), and cytochromes — not Vitamin K.
questions.explanation: Vitamin K is a fat-soluble cofactor for γ-glutamyl carboxylase, an enzyme that converts specific glutamate (Glu) residues to γ-carboxyglutamate (Gla) in target proteins. This post-translational modification enables these proteins to bind Ca²⁺ with high affinity. Key Vitamin K-dependent proteins include: (1) Coagulation factors — prothrombin (II), VII, IX, X, and regulatory proteins C, S, Z (for clotting). (2) Bone proteins — osteocalcin and matrix Gla protein (MGP), important for bone mineralization and vascular calcification prevention.

questions.text: 10. Thiamine gives:
optionReasons: Wrong: T3 (triiodothyronine) and T4 (thyroxine) are thyroid hormones derived from tyrosine and iodine, not from thiamine.
Wrong: CoA (Coenzyme A) is derived from Pantothenic acid (Vitamin B₅), not from thiamine.
Correct: Thiamine (Vitamin B₁) is phosphorylated by thiamine pyrophosphokinase to produce Thiamine Pyrophosphate (TPP), also called thiamine diphosphate (TDP), the active coenzyme form.
Wrong: PLP (Pyridoxal Phosphate) is the active coenzyme form of Pyridoxine (Vitamin B₆), not thiamine.
questions.explanation: Thiamine (Vitamin B₁) is converted in the body to its active coenzyme form, Thiamine Pyrophosphate (TPP), by the enzyme thiamine pyrophosphokinase using ATP. TPP is essential for oxidative decarboxylation of α-keto acids (pyruvate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, branched-chain keto acid dehydrogenase) and for the transketolase reactions of the pentose phosphate pathway.

questions.text: 11. Carboxylation of pyruvate requires:
optionReasons: Wrong: TPP is required for oxidative DEcarboxylation of pyruvate (pyruvate dehydrogenase), not for CARboxylation. These are opposite reactions.
Wrong: B₁₂ (cobalamin) is required for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and methionine synthase reactions, not for pyruvate carboxylation.
Wrong: PLP is the coenzyme for transamination and amino acid decarboxylation reactions, not for CO₂ fixation.
Correct: Pyruvate carboxylation (pyruvate → oxaloacetate) is catalyzed by pyruvate carboxylase, which absolutely requires Biotin as its CO₂-carrying coenzyme. ATP is also required for this reaction.
Wrong: Folic acid (as THF) is the coenzyme for one-carbon transfer reactions (e.g., in purine and thymidylate synthesis), not for carboxylation of pyruvate.
questions.explanation: Pyruvate carboxylase catalyzes: Pyruvate + CO₂ + ATP → Oxaloacetate + ADP + Pᵢ. Biotin is covalently attached to a lysine residue of the enzyme and functions as a mobile CO₂ carrier. In the first step, CO₂ (as bicarbonate) is attached to biotin in an ATP-dependent reaction forming carboxybiotin. In the second step, the carboxyl group is transferred to pyruvate to form oxaloacetate. This reaction is critical for gluconeogenesis and for replenishing TCA cycle intermediates (anaplerosis).

questions.text: 12. THFA is coenzyme for:
optionReasons: Wrong: Transport of amino groups is the function of PLP (pyridoxal phosphate) in transamination reactions, not THFA.
Wrong: CO₂ fixation is the function of Biotin in carboxylation reactions, not THFA.

Correct: Tetrahydrofolic acid (THFA/THF) is the coenzyme for transfer of one-carbon units including methylene (–CH₂–), methyl (–CH₃), formyl (–CHO), and formimino groups in biosynthetic reactions involving purines, thymidylate, serine, methionine, and histidine catabolism.
Wrong: Oxygen transport is the function of hemoglobin and myoglobin (iron-containing proteins), not a vitamin coenzyme.
questions.explanation: Tetrahydrofolate (THF/THFA) is the active coenzyme form of folic acid (Vitamin B₉). It carries and transfers one-carbon units at various oxidation states: (1) N⁵,N¹⁰-methylene-THF — provides the methylene group for dTMP synthesis from dUMP (thymidylate synthase). (2) N⁵-methyl-THF — donates the methyl group to homocysteine for methionine synthesis (requires B₁₂). (3) N¹⁰-formyl-THF — donates formyl groups in de novo purine synthesis. THF deficiency impairs DNA synthesis, leading to megaloblastic anemia.

questions.text: 13. Vitamin E acts as:
optionReasons: Wrong: Anti-rickets activity belongs to Vitamin D, which regulates calcium and phosphate homeostasis essential for bone mineralization.
Wrong: Anti-scurvy activity belongs to Vitamin C (ascorbic acid), which is essential for collagen hydroxylation.
Wrong: Vitamin E has no role in immunoglobulin (antibody) synthesis. Antibodies are proteins produced by B lymphocytes.

Correct: Vitamin E (α-tocopherol) is the principal fat-soluble antioxidant in cell membranes. It donates a hydrogen atom to peroxyl radicals, terminating the lipid peroxidation chain reaction and protecting polyunsaturated fatty acids in membrane phospholipids.
questions.explanation: α-Tocopherol (Vitamin E) is incorporated into cell membranes and lipoprotein particles where it protects polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) from oxidative damage. It reacts with lipid peroxyl radicals (LOO•) to form lipid hydroperoxides (LOOH) and a tocopheroxyl radical (TO•), which is regenerated back to active tocopherol by Vitamin C. This makes Vitamin E the primary chain-breaking antioxidant of biological membranes.

questions.text: 14. Vitamin K is essential for:
optionReasons: Correct: Vitamin K is essential for the post-translational γ-carboxylation of glutamate residues in prothrombin (Factor II), converting it to its active Ca²⁺-binding form necessary for clot formation.
Wrong: Calcitonin is a peptide hormone synthesized by thyroid parafollicular (C) cells in response to hypercalcemia; its synthesis is independent of Vitamin K.
Wrong: Serotonin is synthesized from tryptophan by tryptophan hydroxylase and aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (requires PLP/B₆), not Vitamin K.
Wrong: Catecholamine synthesis (dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine) from tyrosine requires PLP and Vitamin C as cofactors, not Vitamin K.
Wrong: Iron absorption is enhanced by Vitamin C (which reduces Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺) and regulated by hepcidin. Vitamin K plays no role in iron absorption.
questions.explanation: Vitamin K is an absolute requirement for the enzyme γ-glutamyl carboxylase, which performs post-translational carboxylation of specific glutamate residues in prothrombin and other coagulation factors (VII, IX, X) and anticoagulant proteins (C, S). The resulting γ-carboxyglutamate (Gla) residues coordinate Ca²⁺ ions, enabling these proteins to bind to phospholipid surfaces on activated platelets — an essential step in the coagulation cascade leading to fibrin clot formation.

questions.text: 15. Vitamin B₁₂ contains:
optionReasons: Wrong: Iron is the central metal of heme (in hemoglobin, myoglobin, and cytochromes), not of Vitamin B₁₂.
Wrong: Copper is found in ceruloplasmin, cytochrome c oxidase, and superoxide dismutase, not in Vitamin B₁₂.
Wrong: Zinc is a cofactor for carbonic anhydrase, carboxypeptidase, and numerous transcription factors (zinc finger proteins), not a component of B₁₂.
Wrong: Selenium is incorporated into selenoproteins such as glutathione peroxidase and thioredoxin reductase, not into B₁₂.

Correct: Vitamin B₁₂ (cobalamin) contains cobalt (Co) at the center of its corrin ring. The cobalt atom is coordinated by four nitrogen atoms of the corrin tetrapyrrole and forms the basis of all cobalamin biochemistry.
questions.explanation: Vitamin B₁₂ is unique as the only vitamin containing a metallic element — cobalt — which gives it the name cobalamin. The cobalt atom sits within the corrin ring (a contracted tetrapyrrole macrocycle with only three methene bridges, unlike the four in porphyrins). Cobalt can exist in three oxidation states (Co³⁺, Co²⁺, Co¹⁺); the highly nucleophilic Co¹⁺ cob(I)alamin form is the catalytically active species in B₁₂-dependent reactions including methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and methionine synthase.

questions.text: 16. In the regeneration of methionine from homocysteine, which of the following vitamin(s) or vitamin derivative(s) are involved?
optionReasons: Wrong: Lipoic acid is a cofactor in α-keto acid dehydrogenase complexes (pyruvate and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenases), not in methionine regeneration.
Wrong: Retinoic acid is a form of Vitamin A that acts as a nuclear receptor ligand regulating gene transcription. It has no role in homocysteine remethylation.
Wrong: Biotin functions in carboxylation reactions; TPP functions in oxidative decarboxylation. Neither is involved in the methionine cycle.

Correct: Methionine synthase converts homocysteine → methionine using N⁵-methyl-THF (tetrahydrofolate) as the methyl donor and methylcobalamin (Vitamin B₁₂) as an essential cofactor that accepts the methyl group from methyl-THF and transfers it to homocysteine.
Wrong: Vitamins E and K have no biochemical role in the methionine-homocysteine cycle.
questions.explanation: The remethylation of homocysteine to methionine is catalyzed by methionine synthase (also called homocysteine methyltransferase) via two interconnected reactions: (1) N⁵-methyl-THF donates its methyl group to methylcobalamin (methyl-B₁₂). (2) Methylcobalamin then transfers the methyl group to homocysteine, producing methionine and regenerating cob(I)alamin. This reaction is the functional link between folate and B₁₂ metabolism — deficiency of either vitamin impairs methionine synthesis and causes homocysteinemia and megaloblastic anemia.

questions.text: 17. Which one of the following statements concerning vitamin D is CORRECT?
options: A. Hypocalcemia causes direct activation of vitamin D.
B. Hypophosphatemia causes indirect activation of vitamin D.
C. Vitamin D deficiency causes osteomalacia in children.
D. Calcitriol causes normalization of serum calcium by acting on bones, kidney and intestine.
E. Vitamin D opposes the effect of parathyroid hormone.
optionReasons: Wrong: Hypocalcemia activates Vitamin D INDIRECTLY — low Ca²⁺ stimulates PTH secretion, and PTH then activates renal 1α-hydroxylase to produce calcitriol.

Wrong: Hypophosphatemia directly stimulates renal 1α-hydroxylase (and indirectly via FGF-23 suppression), but the question implies it is 'indirect,' which is partially accurate for some pathways. However, option D is the more completely correct statement overall.

Wrong: Vitamin D deficiency causes rickets in CHILDREN (growing bones with defective mineralization at growth plates) and osteomalacia in ADULTS (defective mineralization of newly formed bone matrix). The statement incorrectly applies osteomalacia to children.

Correct: Calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol), the active form of Vitamin D, raises serum calcium by: (1) increasing intestinal Ca²⁺ absorption via calbindin synthesis; (2) promoting renal Ca²⁺ reabsorption; and (3) stimulating osteoclast activity to mobilize Ca²⁺ from bone — all three acting synergistically to normalize serum calcium.
Wrong: Vitamin D and PTH work SYNERGISTICALLY, not antagonistically. Both raise serum calcium. Calcitonin is the hormone that opposes PTH.
questions.explanation: Calcitriol (1,25-(OH)₂-cholecalciferol) is the fully active hormonal form of Vitamin D, produced in the kidney by 1α-hydroxylase (stimulated by PTH, hypocalcemia, and hypophosphatemia). Its three target organs form a coordinated calcium-raising system: (1) Small intestine — calcitriol induces calbindin (calcium-binding protein) synthesis, dramatically increasing transcellular Ca²⁺ absorption. (2) Kidney — promotes Ca²⁺ and phosphate reabsorption in the distal tubule. (3) Bone — stimulates osteoclast differentiation and bone resorption, releasing Ca²⁺ into the bloodstream. Together these actions normalize serum calcium levels.

questions.text: 18. Biotin is coenzyme for:
optionReasons: Correct: Biotin is the coenzyme for all carboxylation (CO₂ fixation) reactions, including pyruvate carboxylase, acetyl-CoA carboxylase, propionyl-CoA carboxylase, and methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase. It functions as a mobile CO₂ carrier.
Wrong: Transamination reactions require PLP (pyridoxal phosphate), not Biotin.
Wrong: Transmethylation reactions require SAM (S-adenosylmethionine) as the methyl donor and involve Vitamin B₁₂ and folate in the methionine cycle, not Biotin.
Wrong: Decarboxylation of α-keto acids requires TPP (thiamine pyrophosphate); amino acid decarboxylation requires PLP. Biotin is specifically for CARboxylation, not DEcarboxylation.
questions.explanation: Biotin is covalently bound to a lysine residue (biocytin) of carboxylase enzymes and functions as a CO₂ carrier. The carboxylation reaction proceeds in two stages: (1) CO₂ (as HCO₃⁻) + ATP + biotin-enzyme → carboxybiotin-enzyme + ADP + Pᵢ (ATP-dependent CO₂ activation). (2) Carboxybiotin-enzyme + substrate → product + biotin-enzyme (CO₂ transfer). Major biotin-dependent enzymes: pyruvate carboxylase (gluconeogenesis), acetyl-CoA carboxylase (fatty acid synthesis), propionyl-CoA carboxylase (odd-chain fatty acid catabolism), and methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase (leucine catabolism).

questions.text: 19. The disease pellagra is due to a deficiency of:
optionReasons: Wrong: Vitamin B₂ (riboflavin) deficiency causes ariboflavinosis, characterized by angular stomatitis, cheilosis, glossitis, and corneal vascularization — not pellagra.
Wrong: Biotin deficiency causes dermatitis, alopecia, and neurological symptoms, but not the classic triad of pellagra.
Wrong: Pantothenic acid deficiency is rare and causes the 'burning feet' syndrome, not pellagra.
Wrong: Folic acid deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and neural tube defects, not pellagra.

Correct: Pellagra is the classic deficiency disease of Niacin (Vitamin B₃), characterized by the four D's: Dermatitis (sun-exposed skin rash), Diarrhea, Dementia, and Death. It can also result from tryptophan deficiency or impaired tryptophan-to-niacin conversion.
questions.explanation: Pellagra results from deficiency of niacin (B₃) and/or its precursor tryptophan. Niacin is required for NAD⁺ and NADP⁺, which are essential for hundreds of metabolic reactions. Deficiency affects rapidly dividing tissues and the nervous system. The photosensitive dermatitis (Casal's necklace pattern on sun-exposed areas), symmetric diarrhea, and neuropsychiatric symptoms (dementia, depression, psychosis) constitute the pellagra syndrome. It is classically seen in populations relying on corn (low in bioavailable niacin and tryptophan) without alkali treatment.

questions.text: 20. Anti-beriberi vitamin is:
optionReasons: Wrong: Riboflavin (B₂) deficiency causes ariboflavinosis with mucosal and skin lesions, not beriberi.

Correct: Beriberi is caused by Thiamine (Vitamin B₁) deficiency. Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) is essential for pyruvate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase. Deficiency impairs aerobic energy metabolism, particularly affecting the nervous system and heart.
Wrong: Ascorbic acid (Vitamin C) deficiency causes scurvy, not beriberi.
Wrong: Nicotinic acid (Niacin/B₃) deficiency causes pellagra, not beriberi.
questions.explanation: Beriberi is the deficiency disease of Thiamine (Vitamin B₁). Two main forms exist: (1) Dry beriberi — peripheral neuropathy with motor and sensory deficits, muscle weakness and wasting. (2) Wet beriberi — high-output cardiac failure with cardiomegaly and peripheral edema due to arteriovenous shunting. Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is the neuropsychiatric form seen in alcoholics. Thiamine is abundant in whole grains; deficiency occurs with polished rice diets or chronic alcoholism.

questions.text: 21. Cobamides are coenzymes derived from:
optionReasons: Wrong: Folic acid gives rise to tetrahydrofolate (THF) coenzymes, not cobamides.
Wrong: Vitamin C functions directly as a reducing cofactor and antioxidant; it does not produce cobamide coenzymes.

Correct: Cobamides (cobalamins) are the coenzyme forms of Vitamin B₁₂. The two active cobamide coenzymes are methylcobalamin (methionine synthase) and adenosylcobalamin/deoxyadenosylcobalamin (methylmalonyl-CoA mutase).
Wrong: Cobalt is the mineral contained within cobamides, but cobamides are derived from the complete vitamin B₁₂ molecule, not from cobalt alone.
Wrong: Nicotinic acid (niacin) gives rise to NAD⁺ and NADP⁺ coenzymes, not cobamides.
questions.explanation: Cobamides are the biologically active coenzyme forms of Vitamin B₁₂ (cobalamin). The term 'cobamide' reflects the cobalt-amide coordination chemistry of the corrin ring. Two principal cobamide coenzymes exist: (1) Methylcobalamin (methyl-B₁₂) — coenzyme for methionine synthase in the cytosol, donating a methyl group to homocysteine. (2) 5'-Deoxyadenosylcobalamin (AdoB₁₂) — coenzyme for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase in mitochondria, converting methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA in odd-chain fatty acid and branched-chain amino acid catabolism.

questions.text: 22. β-Carotene is converted to Vitamin A in the:
optionReasons: Wrong: The liver is the primary storage site for Vitamin A (as retinyl esters in hepatic stellate cells), but the conversion of β-carotene to retinal occurs mainly in the intestine, not the liver.

Correct: β-Carotene is cleaved in intestinal mucosal cells (enterocytes) by the enzyme β-carotene 15,15'-dioxygenase (BCO1) to yield two molecules of all-trans-retinal, which is then reduced to retinol (Vitamin A) for absorption.
Wrong: The spleen is part of the reticuloendothelial system involved in red blood cell destruction and immune function; it plays no role in β-carotene conversion.
Wrong: The adrenal cortex uses Vitamin A for steroidogenesis but does not convert β-carotene to Vitamin A.
Wrong: Adipose tissue stores fat-soluble vitamins including Vitamin A, but does not perform the primary conversion of β-carotene.
questions.explanation: β-Carotene (provitamin A) undergoes central cleavage in the intestinal enterocytes by β-carotene oxygenase (BCO1), producing two molecules of retinal (retinaldehyde). Retinal is then reduced to retinol by retinal reductase. Retinol is esterified to retinyl esters by LRAT (lecithin:retinol acyltransferase) and packaged into chylomicrons for transport via the lymphatic system to the liver, where it is stored as retinyl palmitate in hepatic stellate (Ito) cells.

questions.text: 23. Activation of Vitamin D₃ occurs in:
optionReasons: Wrong: The intestine is a TARGET organ for calcitriol action (inducing calbindin synthesis) but is not involved in the hydroxylation activation steps of Vitamin D.

Correct: Vitamin D₃ (cholecalciferol) undergoes a two-step activation: (1) First hydroxylation at C-25 by 25-hydroxylase (CYP2R1) in the LIVER → 25-hydroxycholecalciferol (calcidiol). (2) Second hydroxylation at C-1 by 1α-hydroxylase (CYP27B1) in the KIDNEY → 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (calcitriol — the active form).
Wrong: Bone is a target organ for calcitriol (stimulating osteoclast activity) but does not perform vitamin D hydroxylation.
Wrong: The kidney performs the second activation step (1α-hydroxylation) but not the first (25-hydroxylation, which occurs in the liver).
Wrong: Bone does not hydroxylate Vitamin D.
questions.explanation: Vitamin D₃ (cholecalciferol) activation requires two sequential hydroxylation steps: Step 1 — In the liver, 25-hydroxylase (CYP2R1, a microsomal enzyme) hydroxylates the C-25 position to form 25-OH-D₃ (calcidiol), the major circulating storage form, carried by vitamin D-binding protein (DBP). Step 2 — In the kidney proximal tubule, 1α-hydroxylase (CYP27B1, mitochondrial) hydroxylates the C-1 position to form 1,25-(OH)₂-D₃ (calcitriol), the biologically active hormone. Renal 1α-hydroxylase is stimulated by PTH, hypocalcemia, and hypophosphatemia, and inhibited by FGF-23 and calcitriol itself (negative feedback).

questions.text: 24. Which one of the following statements concerning vitamin D is CORRECT?
options: A. Chronic renal failure requires administration of 1,25 dihydroxycholecalciferol.
B. Vitamin D is required in the diet of individuals exposed to sunlight.
C. 25-Hydroxycholecalciferol is the active form of the vitamin.
D. Vitamin D opposes the effect of parathyroid hormone.
E. A deficiency of vitamin D results in an increased secretion of calcitonin.
optionReasons: Correct: In chronic renal failure, the kidney cannot perform the crucial 1α-hydroxylation step. Therefore, patients cannot convert 25-OH-D₃ to active 1,25-(OH)₂-D₃ (calcitriol) and must receive the active form (calcitriol/alfacalcidol) directly as a supplement.
Wrong: Individuals with adequate sunlight exposure synthesize sufficient Vitamin D₃ in the skin (from 7-dehydrocholesterol upon UV-B irradiation) and may not require dietary supplementation.

Wrong: 25-hydroxycholecalciferol (calcidiol) is the major CIRCULATING form and is used as a marker of Vitamin D status, but it is NOT the biologically active form. The active form is 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (calcitriol).
Wrong: Vitamin D and PTH are SYNERGISTIC, both acting to raise serum calcium. Calcitonin opposes PTH, not Vitamin D.
Wrong: Vitamin D deficiency causes hypocalcemia → increased PTH secretion (secondary hyperparathyroidism), not increased calcitonin. Calcitonin is secreted in response to HYPERcalcemia.
questions.explanation: Chronic renal failure (CRF) is a major cause of secondary vitamin D deficiency because the kidneys are the sole significant site of 1α-hydroxylation. Loss of functional renal parenchyma → reduced 1α-hydroxylase activity → inability to synthesize calcitriol → secondary hyperparathyroidism, renal osteodystrophy, and hypocalcemia. Treatment requires direct administration of 1,25-(OH)₂-D₃ (calcitriol) or its analogs (alfacalcidol/paricalcitol), bypassing the impaired renal activation step.

questions.text: 25. Skin disorders can occur in case of deficiency of:
options: E. Both retinol and Vitamin K.
optionReasons: Wrong: Niacin deficiency alone causes pellagra with photosensitive dermatitis, but this option is incomplete since retinol deficiency also causes skin disorders.
Wrong: Retinol (Vitamin A) deficiency causes follicular hyperkeratosis and xerosis (dry, rough skin), but this option alone is also incomplete.
Wrong: Vitamin K deficiency causes bleeding disorders (impaired coagulation); it does not primarily cause skin disorders.

Correct: Both niacin deficiency (pellagra — photosensitive dermatitis with hyperpigmentation and desquamation) and retinol deficiency (Vitamin A — follicular hyperkeratosis, 'toad skin'/phrynoderma) cause characteristic skin disorders.
Wrong: Vitamin K deficiency does not cause the skin disorders described; only retinol among the two is correct.
questions.explanation: Two vitamins prominently cause dermatological manifestations when deficient: (1) Niacin (B₃) deficiency — Pellagra dermatitis: bilateral, symmetric, photosensitive rash on sun-exposed areas (face, neck 'Casal's necklace', hands, feet) with hyperpigmentation, scaling, and crusting. (2) Vitamin A (retinol) deficiency — follicular hyperkeratosis (phrynoderma/toad skin): plug formation in hair follicles due to abnormal keratinocyte differentiation, because retinoic acid normally suppresses keratin gene expression and promotes mucus-secreting cell differentiation.

questions.text: 26. The absorption of light by cells in the retina of the eye results in the conversion of:
optionReasons: Wrong: β-Carotene conversion to retinal occurs in the intestinal enterocytes, not in the retina, and is not triggered by light.

Correct: In rod photoreceptors, 11-cis-retinal (bound to opsin as rhodopsin) absorbs a photon of light, causing photoisomerization of 11-cis-retinal to all-trans-retinal. This conformational change activates the opsin protein, initiating the phototransduction cascade.

Wrong: The dark regeneration (visual cycle) involves conversion of all-trans-retinal back to 11-cis-retinal by retinal isomerase in the RPE, but this is NOT caused by light absorption — it occurs in the dark as part of rhodopsin regeneration.
Wrong: Reduction of retinal to retinol by retinol dehydrogenase occurs after bleaching of rhodopsin in the visual cycle, but is not the primary event triggered by light absorption.
Wrong: Oxidation of retinol to retinal (by retinol dehydrogenase in the RPE) is part of the visual cycle regeneration, not the primary light-triggered event.
questions.explanation: The visual cycle in rod cells: (1) 11-cis-retinal combines with opsin (apoprotein) to form rhodopsin (visual purple). (2) Light absorption by rhodopsin causes instantaneous photoisomerization: 11-cis-retinal → all-trans-retinal — this is the primary photochemical event. (3) The conformational change in opsin activates transducin (Gα protein) → phosphodiesterase → cGMP hydrolysis → Na⁺ channel closure → hyperpolarization → visual signal. (4) Regeneration: all-trans-retinal is reduced to all-trans-retinol, transported to RPE, isomerized to 11-cis-retinol, oxidized back to 11-cis-retinal, and returned to combine with opsin.

questions.text: 27. Which of the following characteristics would be seen in a patient with a severe deficiency of thiamine?
options: A. A decreased level of blood pyruvate and lactate.
B. An increased clotting time of blood.
C. A low hepatic cell transaminase activity.
D. A decreased level of transketolase activity in red blood cells.
E. A decreased level of blood calcium.
optionReasons: Wrong: Thiamine deficiency INCREASES blood pyruvate and lactate because pyruvate dehydrogenase (TPP-dependent) is impaired, causing pyruvate accumulation and its conversion to lactate by LDH.
Wrong: Clotting time is affected by Vitamin K deficiency (impaired γ-carboxylation of coagulation factors), not by thiamine deficiency.
Wrong: Transaminase (ALT, AST) activity requires PLP (Vitamin B₆), not TPP. Thiamine deficiency does not reduce hepatic transaminase activity.

Correct: Transketolase in the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) is a TPP-dependent enzyme. Measurement of red blood cell (RBC) transketolase activity — and its activation by exogenous TPP (the TPP effect) — is the most sensitive and specific laboratory test for thiamine deficiency.
Wrong: Blood calcium regulation depends on Vitamin D, PTH, and calcitonin. Thiamine has no direct role in calcium homeostasis.
questions.explanation: Thiamine (B₁) deficiency is classically assessed by measuring erythrocyte transketolase activity. Transketolase catalyzes two reactions in the non-oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway, both requiring TPP. In thiamine deficiency, transketolase activity falls; addition of exogenous TPP in vitro causes >25% stimulation (positive 'TPP effect'), confirming deficiency. Additionally, pyruvate and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complexes (also TPP-dependent) are impaired, causing elevated blood pyruvate, lactate, and α-ketoglutarate — important metabolic markers of thiamine deficiency.

questions.text: 28. Oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate requires:
optionReasons: Correct: TPP (thiamine pyrophosphate) is the essential coenzyme for the E1 component (pyruvate dehydrogenase) of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC), which catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA. The PDC also requires lipoic acid, CoASH, FAD, and NAD⁺.
Wrong: B₁₂ is required for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and methionine synthase, not for pyruvate decarboxylation.
Wrong: PLP is the coenzyme for transamination and amino acid decarboxylation reactions, not for α-keto acid oxidative decarboxylation.
Wrong: Biotin is the coenzyme for CARboxylation (CO₂ addition), the opposite of DEcarboxylation (CO₂ removal).
Wrong: Folic acid (as THF) carries one-carbon units in biosynthetic reactions and has no role in pyruvate oxidative decarboxylation.
questions.explanation: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) catalyzes: Pyruvate + CoASH + NAD⁺ → Acetyl-CoA + CO₂ + NADH. This irreversible reaction uses five coenzymes: (1) TPP (from B₁) — E1 subunit decarboxylates pyruvate and transfers the hydroxyethyl group to lipoic acid. (2) Lipoic acid — E2 swinging arm accepts the acyl group and transfers it to CoA. (3) CoASH (from pantothenic acid) — accepts the acetyl group to form acetyl-CoA. (4) FAD (from riboflavin) — E3 reoxidizes reduced lipoic acid. (5) NAD⁺ (from niacin) — accepts electrons from FADH₂ to form NADH.

questions.text: 29. The vitamin which acts as co-carboxylase is:
optionReasons: Wrong: B₁ (thiamine) acts as co-decarboxylase (as TPP in oxidative decarboxylation of α-keto acids), not as co-carboxylase.
Wrong: B₂ (riboflavin) gives rise to FAD and FMN, which function in oxidation-reduction reactions, not in carboxylation.
Wrong: Niacin gives rise to NAD⁺ and NADP⁺ for electron transfer in oxidoreduction reactions, not carboxylation.

Correct: Biotin functions as co-carboxylase — it is the CO₂-carrying coenzyme in all carboxylation reactions (pyruvate carboxylase, acetyl-CoA carboxylase, propionyl-CoA carboxylase, methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase).
Wrong: B₁₂ functions in methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and methionine synthase reactions, not carboxylation.
questions.explanation: Biotin earns the designation 'co-carboxylase' because it is the prosthetic group of all carboxylase enzymes in mammalian metabolism. Biotin is covalently linked to the ε-amino group of a specific lysine residue in each apocarboxylase, forming biocytin. The bicyclic ring of biotin (ureido + tetrahydrothiophene) accepts CO₂ at the N-1 position of the ureido ring (forming carboxybiotin) in an ATP-dependent half-reaction, then transfers the CO₂ to the substrate in the second half-reaction.

questions.text: 30. Decarboxylation of glutamate requires:
optionReasons: Wrong: TPP is required for oxidative decarboxylation of α-keto acids (pyruvate, α-ketoglutarate, branched-chain keto acids) — not for amino acid decarboxylation.
Wrong: B₁₂ has no role in glutamate decarboxylation; it functions in methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and methionine synthase reactions.

Correct: Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) is the essential coenzyme for glutamate decarboxylase (GAD), which catalyzes the decarboxylation of glutamate → GABA (γ-aminobutyric acid), the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS.
Wrong: Biotin catalyzes the reverse reaction — carboxylation (CO₂ addition) — not decarboxylation.
Wrong: Folic acid (THF) is involved in one-carbon transfer reactions, not in amino acid decarboxylation.
questions.explanation: PLP (pyridoxal phosphate) is the coenzyme for amino acid decarboxylases, including glutamate decarboxylase (GAD), which produces GABA from glutamate. In all PLP-dependent decarboxylations, PLP forms a Schiff base (aldimine) with the α-amino group of the amino acid substrate. The electron-withdrawing capacity of the PLP-pyridinium system facilitates loss of the α-carboxyl group as CO₂, producing the corresponding amine. PLP deficiency impairs GABA synthesis, leading to neuronal hyperexcitability and convulsions.

questions.text: 31. Vitamin E is a substance that:
optionReasons: Wrong: Rancidity is caused by oxidative degradation of unsaturated fatty acids by free radicals and oxygen. Vitamin E prevents rather than causes this process.

Correct: Vitamin E (α-tocopherol) prevents rancidity by acting as a chain-breaking antioxidant. It donates a hydrogen atom to lipid peroxyl radicals (LOO•), terminating the lipid peroxidation chain reaction that causes rancidity in oils and food products.
Wrong: Hardening of oils is achieved by hydrogenation (catalytic addition of H₂ to double bonds), which is an industrial process unrelated to Vitamin E.
Wrong: Emulsification of oils requires amphipathic molecules such as bile salts, lecithin, or detergents. Vitamin E has no emulsifying properties.
questions.explanation: Rancidity in fats and oils results from free-radical chain reactions (lipid peroxidation) that oxidatively degrade polyunsaturated fatty acids, producing unpleasant odors and flavors (aldehydes, ketones). Vitamin E (α-tocopherol) is the most important natural lipid-soluble antioxidant that prevents rancidity both in biological systems (cell membranes) and in food preservation. The phenolic OH group of the chroman ring donates H• to peroxyl radicals, stopping the chain reaction. The resulting tocopheroxyl radical is relatively stable and can be regenerated by Vitamin C.

questions.text: 32. Which of the following stimulates the synthesis of calcium-binding protein in intestinal mucosa?
optionReasons: Wrong: Luminal calcium does not directly induce calbindin synthesis; it is the hormonal signal (calcitriol) that does so via nuclear receptor-mediated gene transcription.

Correct: Calcitriol (1,25-(OH)₂-D₃) binds to the Vitamin D receptor (VDR) in intestinal enterocytes, and the calcitriol-VDR complex acts as a nuclear transcription factor that upregulates the gene encoding calbindin-D (calcium-binding protein), dramatically increasing intestinal calcium absorption.
Wrong: Calcitonin is secreted by thyroid C-cells in response to hypercalcemia and acts primarily to inhibit osteoclastic bone resorption. It does not stimulate intestinal calbindin synthesis.
Wrong: α-Tocopherol (Vitamin E) is an antioxidant and has no role in calcium transport or calbindin regulation.
